I bow to that unique Goddess, the self-awareness of one's own nature, within whom this entire universe shines as an external appearance during manifestation; yet when agitation has ceased, she remains as the unsurpassed state.

I bow to that Supreme, Unsurpassed, and self-luminous Splendor— the wonder of intuitive insight— which, having established within the heart the Triad consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, causes it to shine forth.
Victorious is the illustrious primordial teacher Śambhu, the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, whose greatness is priceless and who has liberated the multitude of bound souls.
For the sake of awakening my own disciples and for the remembrance of the Awakened One,
I, Abhinavagupta, exert this slight effort.
Paratriṃśikā 1:
The Goddess said:
O God, how is the Unsurpassed (anuttara) the immediate bestower of Kaulika perfection?
By the mere knowledge of which, one attains equality with the sky-farer (khecarī).

The Supreme Lord, whose nature consists of the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*), is eternally pervaded by His supreme form of power (*parā-śakti*) which consists of grace (*anugraha*); in reality, He is essentially one with grace alone, for power cannot be conceived as distinct from Śiva. And that power, consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of grace toward the worlds, is initially differentiated into hundreds of infinite powers that are about to be projected within *paśyantī*, which consists of reflective awareness.

First of all, it is firmly established in consciousness (*saṃvit*) which consists of the supreme mantra (*paramahāmantra*) and is untouched by space or time; at that stage, it exists precisely without the distinction between the speech and response that will later arise in *paśyantī*.
And that very [consciousness], consisting of the non-duality of the consciousness of all subjects, exists eternally in the form of the present.
From that [state], however, Paśyantī reflects—merely by the threading of awareness—that which is desired, once it has been awakened by the determination of appropriate causes;

just as memory reflects only a certain thing from a variegated cognition (mecakadhi) conditioned by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the knowledge of various entities and absences, due to the suitability of awakening the seeds of memory.
For at the time of the first cognition, no distinction flashes forth wherein there would be non-difference between the specific signified and the signifier;

however, the intermediate speech (madhyamā) manifests the distinction between those very two—the signified and the signifier—and functions as a reflective awareness through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); whereas the articulated speech (vaikharī), on the other hand...

Since it is established by one's own self-awareness that [the ultimate] consists precisely in the manifestation of the distinction between those two, that very ground of Parāvāc is— in fact— situated even in the subsequent stages such as Paśyantī; for its essence is the non-conventional, uncreated, and ultimate refinement (*saṃskāra*) which is the true nature of the power of the word within the realm of Māyā, and it is impelled by the portion that constitutes the vitality (*vīrya*) of mantra according to the method to be described hereafter.
Without her, there would be the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatā*) due to the resulting lack of manifestation in the [powers] beginning with *paśyantī*;
and in that state, no differentiation whatsoever—such as "this," "thus," "here," or "now"—could exist.

Therefore, starting from the form of the emission of the supreme great vitality (*vīrya*) of Mantra, up to the manifestation of the distinctions of objective states (*bhāva*) as they unfold in *vaikharī*, [all this occurs through her].

When this [consciousness], consisting of its own self-manifestation, abides within itself— which is pure luminosity— and vibrates, that very vibration is the "I," whose ultimate reality is uninterruptedness.
This will become clear further on.
Precisely in the midst of that, where there is the non-projection of the aspect of differentiation in Paśyantī, and where there is the manifestation of differentiation in Madhyamā—

in both those forms consisting of the powers of knowledge and action, which are the essence of Sadāśiva and Īśvara— there is that very wonder of "I," whose internal activity is full of the wonder of the infinite variety of all internal objects. This is the nature of that Paśyantī and Madhyamā.
In reality, one contemplates one's very own self as consisting of supreme consciousness;
and this supreme consciousness itself is called the Blessed Goddess.

To this extent, by means of this play whose nature is the bliss of self-reflection, proceeding through the sequence of emanation beginning with Paśyantī and extending to external objects such as blue, etc., [the Lord acts].

Because the Blessed Lord Bhairava abides in a state of supreme excellence by virtue of transcending all things, and because he desires to abide in that manner through the impulse of the will to conquer (*vijigīṣā*),
by means of performing such worldly transactions as infinite knowledge, memory, doubt, and certainty, and by manifesting—
as the very nature of the manifestation of blue and so forth— within everything that appears, such as blue and the like; [he is the Supreme].
Because he is praised by all through their immersion in his very light and their inclination toward it,
and because he attains the state of being the self of all at will, unconditioned by space and time;
for this very reason, the status of deity is primarily attributed to Bhairavanātha alone.
The state of being the Goddess (devī-rūpatā) belongs precisely to that power (tac-chakti) of the Blessed One.
As it has been said: "The root *div* [is used] in the senses of playing, desiring victory, worldly transaction, splendor, praise, and movement.

And thus, because they partake in even a fraction of the grace of such a deityhood consisting of supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*), Viṣṇu, Viriñci, and others are conventionally designated as "deities" (*devatā*). In this way...

When the Bhagavatī—Paśyantī and Madhyamā—contemplates her very own self, thinking, "I am indeed the goddess Parāvāk; thus have I spoken," then, by virtue of that form, through the emergence of Māyā, and because of its dependence upon her own self, she follows the differentiation belonging to that Māyā and identifies that very same supreme state (parābhūmi), which consists of her own self, as being an externalized object.

Because it transcends the path of the internal and external organs—which are animated by the manifestation of duality—it is perceived as remote (parokṣatayā), since it is not delimited by the present time defined by the divisions of day dependent on the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies.
A day for Brahmā is measured by many kalpas,

and for Viṣṇu and others, it is even longer than that; yet, at the end [of their cycles], even when the movement of the vital breath has reached a hundred-thousandth part of its course, there is still the conventional usage of "day"— thus, time is unstable and merely conceptual.

According to the principle that "how could there be contemporaneity in the non-conceptualized nature of consciousness?", one should reflect by means of the sequence of the third person singular and the remote past tense, thereby fulfilling the sense of a past event that is not contemporary or perceptible:
"I myself am she, that very goddess of supreme speech, insofar as all signified objects and signifying words are undivided."
This is the intended meaning:
"I was indeed asleep and I spoke"—this alone is the logical conclusion. For one does not remember that past state, because it was previously unperceived.

Now, through the majesty recounted by another person, or through the onset of bodily transformations such as stammering produced by acts like excessive lamentation and singing, one attains that state through wonder (*camatkāra*).
For this is not merely a lack of cognition;

for in states such as intoxication, sleep, or fainting, there is a state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) because of the non-apprehension of specific objects of knowledge, as in the thought, "I indeed lamented while intoxicated or asleep."

In the state of *parā*, however, there is simply an absence of any specific object of cognition (*vedya-viśeṣa*), because here [the subject] consists of the fourth state (*turya*) due to the realization of identity with the cognizer (*vedaka-tādātmya*); whereas in states such as intoxication and the like, there is a predominance of the onset of delusion (*moha-āveśa*). This is the distinction.

But their state of being beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*) is exactly the same. Thus, every cognizer (*pramātṛ*), whether situated in the roles of teacher, disciple, and so forth, or in any other worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), at all times, while performing whatever action, enters into this very consciousness and becomes the vessel for all transactions.
Therefore, she reflects upon that very reality in its true nature; thus the Goddess said:

"As long as it may be said that I alone constantly reflect upon everything non-differentially on the level of Parā, otherwise this clear manifestation occurring on the levels of Paśyantī and Madhyamā would not exist."
By this alone it is meant that "the Goddess said";
in the same way, it should be understood that earlier it was "Bhairava said.
For even there, the meaning is that it was Bhairava himself—the self whose nature consists of the non-differentiation of his own power and other powers—who said "I said."
When there is the reflective awareness (amarśa) of the nature of emanation, characterized primarily by Śakti, the appropriate reflective awareness of the Goddess is "I" (aham);
when there is the reflective awareness of absorption in withdrawal, characterized primarily by the possessor of Śakti (Śaktimat), the aesthetic wonder of the form of Bhairava is "Maha" (mahaḥ).
This will be clarified later.

Furthermore, this is the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the supreme consciousness—which consists of the power of will—within the sphere of the *paśyantī* and *madhyamā* levels, which consist of the power of knowledge;
and that alone is the purpose of the entire treatise, from its commencement to its conclusion.

Therefore, within the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) itself, which consists of Sadāśiva, the conjunction of words and sentences—such as *da*, *e*, *va*, *ya*, *au*, *va*, *ā*, *ca*, *bha*, *ai*, *ra*, *a*, *va*, *a*, and so forth—arises from the manifestation of the sequence of preceding and succeeding words and sentences; it is indeed the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the true, supreme potency of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*).
And it is said in the *Svacchandatantra*:
Q: "Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through sentences consisting of preceding and following words" (SvaTa 8.31).

Thus, the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*) is eternally unceasing within all subjects; therefore, this very supreme relationship (*para-sambandha*) is the sole life-force of the scripture that is the essence of the Trika (*ṣaḍardha*).

In this unsurpassed [reality], because of the teaching already stated, there is a state of supreme oneness (*paraikamayatva*) regarding other types of relations—such as the great intervals between the divine and the non-divine and so forth.
As it is said in the *Trikahṛdaya*:
"The Supreme Lord is eternally intent upon emission within His own power."
