That very [reality], when touched upon in the state of Paśyantī with the desire to differentiate letters, words, and sentences, and established as distinct in the stage of Madhyamā, becomes the objective reality that precedes all things, extending down to Vaikharī—the unsurpassed [state] which culminates in the arrangement of letters, words, and sentences belonging to the differentiated Māyā, such as "How? and so forth.
This very [reality] is that unperceivable mouth of Bhairava, whose essence consists of the reflective awareness of emanation.

The primordial *dhruvapada* (the fixed word), which is the seed of the expansion of the Trika scriptures, consists of the arousal (*kṣobha*) arising from the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*) of Śiva and Śakti—the forms of whose essence are the unsurpassed state of "I-ness" (*anuttarāhaṃbhāva*). It is the sole life-force of all living beings.
Therefore, because there is no differentiation and because designations such as "place" (*sthāna*) are inapplicable, it is not logical for it to be preceded by place and so forth.
As for the reality (*vastu*), which takes the form of the question and its answer, it is eternally manifest from the very beginning, consisting of non-differentiation.

Therefore, this is the essential point here: one's own Self, which is the intrinsic nature of all things, while manifesting itself, contemplates its own Self by means of questions and answers that are non-different from the Self—questions and answers consisting of the Self as the questioner and respondent, and characterized by the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*)—thereby experiencing wonder. This amounts to saying: "Desiring such manifold wonders, I, knowing it thus, become exactly so. To this extent, the Goddess said:

Beginning with "How is it unsurpassed? and continuing from Bhairava’s words "Listen, O Goddess" up to "Thus is the Rudrayāmala," or else including all the scriptures beginning with the *Pañcasrotas* down to this worldly convention— this is what is called the supreme connection (*para-sambandha*).
I, Abhinavagupta, have constantly explained this secret essence of instruction, which brings about the state of Bhairava immediately— the *Praśnasarvasva*, the treasury of all questions.
Out of a desire for the welfare of our disciples, however, we shall summarize and state this very point:
whatever is to be known and whatever is to be done in all worldly transactions,
that unfolds, free from differentiation, in the supreme fourth stage (turyabhūmi).

In the *paśyantī* state, which consists of the subtle outlining of differentiation and possesses a sequential nature, [the sequence] exists internally; in the *madhyamā* state, that same sequence, characterized by differentiation, lacks internal clarity.
Then, having intensely meditated upon the intermediate and the supreme [states] as non-different from one another,
one should contemplate that very moment as if it were imperceptible, like one who is intoxicated or asleep.
In this very way, he will explain this state of unsurpassedness.
This has been stated by the venerable Śrī Somānandapāda in his own commentary on the *Parātriṃśikā*:
"Immediately after the first spanda of Śakti, of the Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka who is intent upon the fivefold act," and so forth.
This effort of ours—who have been sanctified by that teaching—is precisely for the purpose of crushing that knot.
The connection has been stated. The subject matter is the *Triṃśikā*.

The Goddess is the sovereign (īśvarī) of the three powers— will, knowledge, and action— which are otherwise designated as emanation and so forth; and since this lordship exists only as non-different from that which is to be ruled, the Blessed Lady Bhaṭṭārikā, who transcends these three divisions of power and consists of the inseparability of those powers, is the supreme reality to be denoted,
and it is precisely through union with her that this [text] serves as its designation.
The teachers also read it as *triṃśakā*;

and because of the similarity in phonemes and letters, they provide this etymological explanation (*nirukta*): it is called *triṃśakā* because it "brings forth" (*kāyati*) the three powers (*tisraḥ śaktīḥ*), and not *triṃśikā* because of its connection with thirty verses.
Even though it is so extensive, it possesses thirty topics; for thus it is said in the *Śrītantrasāra*:
"The thirty topics have been proclaimed by you, with an extent of one and a half crores. [TaSā]
Thus, the relationship between the signifier and the signified is indeed one of identity (*tādātmya*), as has been largely explained;

and the purpose [of this teaching] is for all cognizers who, by virtue of the grace of the supreme descent of power (*para-śaktipāta*), have become vessels for this much of the unsurpassed knowledge (*anuttara-jñāna*).

For them, through the internalization of their own essential nature (*nijasvarūpa*) in this manner, the entire multitude of principles—which are considered bonds—have their duality illuminated by the play of the abundance of their own innate fragrance.
Liberation while living consists of an immersion (*samāveśa*) into the non-dual nature of Bhairava, which is the identity with the *ahantā* (I-consciousness) full of the wonder of one's own Self.

For it is proclaimed that liberation from what is considered bondage occurs for one who is firmly rooted—even within the sphere of the vital breath, the body, and the external objects of the senses—in that state called "impulsion" (*preraṇā*), which takes the form of exertion, power, life-force, and so forth.
Indeed, even when the mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of Māyā have been severed, what kind of verbal expression of "liberation" could this possibly be?
Or with respect to what?
As it has been said in the *Śrīspanda*:
"He whose consciousness perceives the entire universe as a play..."
Q: "Seeing thus, constantly disciplined, he is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt" (SpaKā 2.5).
And this will become clear very shortly. [ , . . . . . , . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

] Therefore, since the purpose here is precisely this self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the ultimate consummation of all human goals, there is no room for a further purpose beyond this purpose.
The relationship, the subject matter, and the purpose have already been stated.
Now, the meaning of the text is explained:
"unsurpassed" (anuttara).
[1. There exists nothing superior or further beyond it;

for, just as the thirty-six other principles, culminating in Anāśritaśiva, enhance consciousness by attaining such a state of perfection through entering into the awakening of Supreme Bhairava, so it is not with the supreme, perfectly full consciousness of Supreme Bhairava.
[2. Because its essence consists in the wonder of a perpetually self-manifesting expansion that is unimpeded and independent;
likewise, there exists no "answer" (uttara) in the form of a response to a question therein.

For it is precisely from the great ocean of consciousness—which is the infinite abode of surging creative intuition—that the disciple becomes a vessel for the emergence of questions, insights, and so forth.
Since that very reality is in fact eternally manifest, what other answer could there be from the Teacher?
"Crossing over" (*uttara*) refers to liberation (*apavarga*), which is intended by those who advocate for differentiation;
for that, in reality, does not transcend being animated by necessity (*niyati*).
For it is thus: first, having entered from the body into the plane of vital breath (*prāṇa*),
then having ascended from that to the plane of intellect (*buddhi*),
and even from that to the state called vibration (*spandana*).
Having superimposed the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*),

and from that state having ascended to the level of the void (*śūnya*) which consists in the dissolution of all objects of cognition, and further, upon reaching the culmination of the progressive attenuation of all impurities, the individual soul (*aṇu*) is liberated through the manifestation of its Śiva-nature, because the superimposition has thereby become purposeless.

[4. The "higher" (*uttara*) refers to the sequence of ascending further upward, attained through the successive stages of presiding over the centers (*adhiṣṭhāna*) beginning with the navel, heart, throat, palate, the abode of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), and Bhairava. [5. Likewise, because one ascends by means of it, it is the "higher" bond (*bandha*).
[6. The "higher" is the crossing-over; it is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus, where there are no such further [qualifications],
and where there is a verbal designation (*śabdana*),
that would effect an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) in every way, such as "it is exactly like this" or "it is like that."
Therefore, that which does not exist as uninterrupted is this "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*).
For even the notion "this" has its very life in the exclusion of other subsequent exclusions; thus, because it functions as an exclusion, it is essentially conceptual (*vikalpātman*).

Consequently, as long as the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātṛ*) desires to enter into the form of the unsurpassable, he remains entirely within the imagined nature (*kalpita*), characterized by specific distinctions.
In that regard, however, that which is non-conceptualized and inseparable [from reality] is precisely what is ultimately supreme, because without it, the conceptualized form does not manifest.

For in that case, the non-occurrence of cultivation and so forth is indeed due to the nature of reality itself; thus it is said to be devoid of the operation of cultivation, and not merely because of its uselessness.
Such is this unsurpassed [reality], which remains exactly so even within the functions of conventional discourse.
This has been stated by me myself in a hymn:
"Just as a mass of water falling very slowly across the vast sky is not perceived because it is unbroken,
yet it becomes clearly visible due to its proximity to the branches of garden trees, houses, and mountain slopes."
In the same way, O Questioner:
the Supreme Bhairava, due to its extreme subtlety, never at all comes within the range of experience.
Q: Now, [the following are] the conjunctions of being a maker through the arrangement of place, form, and time, and through stability and motion.
For they, generating the experiencing consciousness, instantly suppress the awakening of Bhairava.
And so it will be stated: "The answer to the answer as well. This is also explained:
"In this very way, the Śākta answer belongs to the individual soul (nārātman), and beyond that is the Śāmbhava."

Likewise, even within those [elements], there is a successive progression within one's own self through the distinctions of the elements, reality, the self, the mantra-lords, and the powers; and even among the elements and so forth, there is a succession such as earth and the rest— for instance, the dream state follows the waking state.
From that comes deep sleep,
from that the fourth state, and beyond that, the state transcending that.
Even within the states of waking and so forth, there is a successive progression within one's own self through the differentiation of the four [states] and the rest;
this has been determined by me in detail in the *Śrīpūrvapañcikā*, but it is not explained here at length because it is of no use in this context and would result in excessive prolixity.
Such is this state of "subsequent-ness" (*uttaratva*), which produces the delusion of duality regarding the hierarchy of higher and lower.
Likewise, there should be no deficiency or excess regarding the division of castes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of the lowest birth.
There is a predominance of the abstract state (bhāva) in the subsequent term; "the subsequent" refers to the powers such as Paśyantī and the others, as well as Aghora and the rest.
Those beginning with *parā* and so forth;
where those do not occur: [13. from the root *nud* in the sense of "impelling," *nut* is the act of impelling (*nodana*).
By means of that, crossing occurs through the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*);
the consciousness of the disciple is impelled by the consciousness of the Guru.

Through that, according to the succession of distinctions between locations—such as the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the void (*śūnya*), and the equinox (*viṣuvat*)—he performs the initiation that bestows liberation, whether in the state with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), by means of the application of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and other rites.
Therefore, in this case, how can these mockeries apply to consciousness, which is self-luminous, all-pervading, and not differentiated by specific spatial or temporal forms?
Thus, that in which there is no crossing over by means of such a push or impulsion is "without answer" (*anuttara*).
As it will be said:

Q: "For one who knows this in its true essence, there arises initiation leading to Nirvāṇa... [verse 25]. [14. Regarding the term *aṇu*: from the root *an* (to breathe) and *svas* (to breathe), with the suffix *kvip*, *aṇu* refers to the self (*ātman*), such as the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) and so forth.
Likewise, non-speaking is life (*jīvana*).
Life is a function (*vṛtti*) consisting primarily of a void egoity (*ahaṃtā*), which is distinct from various powers and so forth, and which resides within the body and other [faculties];
this is what is called the "void subject" (*śūnyapramātā*).
Its "superiority" (uttaratvam) consists in its being supreme over all things by virtue of its ultimate reality, because it is composed solely of Bhairava.
In this world filled with both the insentient and the sentient, [ordinary beings] remain as insentient entities, submerged within the single life-force.
And as for the "life" of those who live, it has been stated previously:
it is the single supreme sovereignty of the Lord, consisting of knowledge and action, which belongs to all;
for even in other cases, the body and so forth appear as distinct entities only by virtue of that [sovereignty], just as one's own self does.
Furthermore, that which is the act of breathing is self-luminous precisely through non-differentiation.
And this alone is the ultimate reality, as stated by the venerable Utpaladeva:
"Knowledge and action are considered the life-force of living beings."

[Thus ends Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.14. Likewise, life is nothing other than knowledge and action. [15. And this "A" is that which consists of the wonder of one's own self—the waveless ocean of consciousness resting in the great, natural, non-illusory, and non-scriptural Great Light.

The *kalā* (aspect) which resides on both levels—the first of which culminates in the full *ahambhāva* (I-consciousness) whose nature is the reflective awareness (*amarśana*) of the universe consisting of the unfolding of power (*śāktollāsa*)—is that very [aspect] whose "propulsion" (*nud*) is its state of ending in emission (*visarga*), as will be explained later. Its "crossing over" (*taraḥ*) is its floating, its state of revolving above all things. That in which there is no "propulsion" (*nut*)—meaning no impulse consisting of sequential action dependent on duality such as movement to and from space and time—is "anud" (non-propelled), according to common worldly usage, referring to space and so forth.
Even more excellent than that is the unsurpassed [consciousness].

For even in the case of space and so forth, such a sequential activity might indeed occur due to the influence of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as pots which possess conjunction, and due to their connection with inherent qualities (*samavāyin*) such as sound;

however, in the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which consists essentially of the sovereignty of all-pervasive, unconditioned, and perfect autonomy, and in which any potentially suspected limiting adjunct has been assimilated through a repose consisting of uninterrupted wonder, [no such sequence exists].

In the Self, which is without appearance yet eternally manifest, and which has rendered non-manifestness into a mere appearance by its own acceptance, there is a flood of all possible states of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

Because there is no sequence dependent on space and time—since both the manifestation of "this-ness" and its non-manifestation are essentially [identical]—there exists only the non-sequential activity known as *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), consisting of the intense impulse of self-contemplation, as well-known in traditions such as the *Matsyodarīmata*. That alone is the Absolute (*anuttara*).
The suffix *tamap* is prescribed for mere excellence (*atiśayamātra*), whereas *tarap* is used here when there is a dual number or a word expressing division (*dvivacanavibhajyopapada*).
For example: "This one is white, and this one is white."

In the sentence "This is the whitest among these two," the meaning is: "Between these two white things, this one is the whitest, i.e., whiter (*śuklatara*). But what is this additional meaning [in the case of the plural] such as: "Among these white things, this one is the whitest"?
For instance, it is like saying, "This palace is white."
"This cloth is white,
this swan is also white, and among these, this one is the most exceedingly white."
In that case, since both the palace is white and the cloth is white, what would be said as something additional?
Even with respect to that suffix, the formulation of such a sentence would be entirely improper; nor indeed would the *tamap* suffix denote a greater degree (*atiśaya*) than the *tarap* suffix.
Thus, it may be that the suffix *tamap* is used when the specific counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not intended to be expressed,
whereas *tarap* is used when there is a requirement for a specific counter-correlative.
The very requirement of a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) constitutes the meaning of the dual number and the word used as a basis for division;
for there can be only one counter-correlative.
Of these two, this...
The third [alternative]— that "white" is [the most] preeminent— is not understood,

because by means of the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it is perceived that only the first [term] functions as the correlative (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, there can be no simultaneous dependence on two or more [terms] for a single [entity].
Since each [term] is considered to depend on its predecessor, there is no additional meaning for it in its sequence.

However, the usage "tāratamya" (gradation) is simply unestablished in the sense of a progression of sequence; for if it followed the meaning of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, then forms such as *tārya* and *tāmya* would also have to occur.
Therefore, enough with this display of mere proficiency in a fragmentary scriptural citation out of context.
However, in this case, when there is a requirement for a subsequent counter-correlative, even in the usage of the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*), the meaning is precisely this same one.
For it is said thus in another scripture:

Q: "That which even now is not known to the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who possess awakening, yet there is nothing whatsoever that remains unknown to anyone—this is the unsurpassed. Thus, the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) has as its body the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which is permeated by the essence of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
Thus it has been said by the venerable Utpaladeva:
"The sequential nature of worldly action is possible due to the power of time, but not so for the eternal action belonging to the Lord, which is like that of the Sovereign. [IPK 2.1.2]
Thus it has been explained; this unsurpassed [reality] is sixteenfold. As it is stated in the *Sāraśāstra*:
"The Unsurpassed is that Heart; its nature as a knot resides within the heart."
Q: "Having known the knot to be sixteenfold, one should perform action as one pleases" [Trikasāra?].
Likewise:
Q: "The knot which resides in the heart [is that which regulates above and below],"
"Consciousness," etc., as stated in the *Mālinīsāra* (IPVV 3, p. 293).
In what manner is that unsurpassed state such? Is it by the abandonment of the form of the "surpassed," or rather otherwise?
And what is this manner, whereby all this collection of knowledge and the objects of knowledge—which everywhere consists of mutual differentiation—experiences contradiction?
Therefore, this superiority or inferiority must indeed exist;
and in what manner does it occur—is it in liberation itself, or even in that which is considered bondage?
Since the suffix *tham* is prescribed to denote a mere manner (prakāra) without restriction to any specific case-meaning (*vibhakti*), this question refers exclusively to a mere manner.
"Deva" has already been explained.

"Kula" refers to the nature of a collection consisting of gross and subtle [elements], the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the senses (*indriya*), the elements (*bhūta*), and so forth, due to their relationship as cause and effect;
as it has been said: "because they act through combination."
Likewise, *kula* is so called because consciousness itself abides in a state of congealed form, and because of its very freedom as consciousness, it conceives of itself as bound.
For it is said that *kula* means "conglomeration" (*saṃstyāna*) and "relatives" (*bandhu*).
Indeed, apart from being of the single nature of consciousness whose sole essence is light, no unmanifested body of these [entities] is possible.

In that context, *kaulikī siddhi* is the state existing within the *kula*, which is the firmness of suchness (*tathātva-dārḍhya*), having the nature of the bliss of final liberation (*parinirvṛti-ānanda-rūpa*), and consisting of identity with the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Śiva, whose essence is the supreme consciousness that is the very nature of the Heart.
It bestows that accomplishment.
For when there is identity with the nature of the Absolute (*anuttara-svarūpa-tādātmya*), the *kula* becomes such. As it has been said:
Q: For the determination of what is other and what is not other occurs through exclusion and non-exclusion;
furthermore, establishment, foundation, accomplishment, and fulfillment are said to be synonymous.
[From the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi* 12]:

Thus, the word "sadyas" (immediately) has the meaning "on the same day" according to the stated method; however, because the day is not fixed [in its duration], it functions here in the sense of "in the same moment.
Furthermore, the sameness of the moment does not consist in similarity.
Rather, it culminates precisely in reality;
in this very way, the cognition arises from the word *sadyas*.
Therefore, by the phrase "in that very moment," the present moment is delimited, thereby excluding other past and future moments.

One should also cast off the temporality of the present, which has its life-force (*prāṇa*) in the calculation dependent upon both [past and future], since this "Kula"— described as consisting of the circle of rays of the Supreme Lord Bhairava, whose nature is the expansion of his own light—
reaches a state of cessation characterized by identity with the inward-turned consciousness of the supreme Bhairava.
Then, that very [state] consists of the tasting of the nectar of supreme bliss; it is undivided by space or time, unsurpassed, eternal, of the nature of emission (*visarga*), and perpetually arisen.
As it is said in the venerable *Vādyatantra*:
"Having restrained one's own wheel of rays and having drunk the unsurpassed nectar..."
Q: One who is not delimited by either time [past or future] shall be happy in the present.
[From the *Śrīvādyatantra*? / Cited in the *Mālinīvijayavārttika* 1.156 as attributed to the *Ḍāmaratantra*].
And the non-delimitation of both time [and space] has been elaborated at length elsewhere by me alone.

Likewise, the *siddhi* (accomplishment) that has come from the *kula*—from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the body, and so forth—is that which bestows the form of certainty regarding the differentiated entities such as blue, pleasure, and so on.

For the body and other factors, through the sudden penetration of the power of the unsurpassed, eternal emission (*anuttara-dhruva-visarga-vīrya-āveśa*)—which is untouched by time—perform the accomplishment consisting of the certainty of the true nature of all things simply by ascending the middle ladder of the vital breath and so forth.
As it has been said:
Q: "But rather, through contact with the power of the Self, a person may become equal to That" (Spandakārikā 1.8).
Likewise: "...
like the sense organs of embodied beings..."

[Spandakārikā 2.10] Thus, although Śiva and Śakti are present within the Kula, the aforementioned accomplishment— which consists of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā) and is the ground for producing the desired powers such as *aṇimā*—
bestows that state immediately, even without being conceptualized, precisely because it is devoid of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), ritual instruments (*karaṇa*), and so forth.
As it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānandapāda:
"What need is there for meditation or ritual action for Śiva, who is eternally manifest? (Śivadṛṣṭi 8.5,6).
Likewise...
Q: Once, through valid means, from a scripture, or from the words of a guru, when Śiva-nature—which resides in all things—has been known with firm conviction, [one attains liberation].
Q: "There is no purpose whatsoever for an instrument, nor even for contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). [Śivadṛṣṭi 7.556?

Thus, the accomplishment born of the Kula—from the initial expansion of forms such as the Śākta and Hādi, up to the blossoming of the veil of external existence—is the manifestation of duality; it bestows that [accomplishment].

For that very [reality] is the unsurpassed (*anuttara*), whose nature is Great Light, which has internalized the expansion of all objective existences consisting of consciousness. Precisely because it is unsurpassed, due to the intensity of the wonder of its peerless sovereign freedom, it [manifests] duality...
It causes [it] to blossom.
For that which is not of the nature of light could not be the cause for the manifestation of the blossoming of an entity.
If it is of the nature of light, then it is certainly the very form of the Supreme Lord, Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka; what is the use of further webs of words?

Likewise, that by which the measures (*mātrā*)— which consist of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*)— are known through supreme distinction as protection, preservation, and lordship by means of the measure (*māna*) and the self as knower (*pramātman*),
that is "that by which the measures are known" (*vijñātāmātra*). Likewise, that which is known through the bond of firmness in realization is indeed fully manifest (*vibhāta*).
Furthermore, it does not require further cultivation because its nature is eternally manifest;
likewise, as soon as it is known, it is indeed known, because the object of knowledge has a single form,
whereas a jar or similar object is never of the nature of the knower.
Likewise, this māyā consists of duality, comprising both the knower and the object of knowledge;
that in which both of these have ceased is pure consciousness alone (vijñānamātra).
In that state where objects such as jars possess the nature of self-luminosity by virtue of being of one form with the knower,
and where Māyā has no power,
[the world is known] merely by that consciousness.

Abiding in the void (*kha*) which is Brahman in its undifferentiated form, it moves—that is, it perceives objects—and likewise performs activities such as rejecting or accepting; yet it also remains in its own essential nature. Thus, *khecarī* consists of the internal and external senses, their objects, pleasure, and forms such as blue. For instance, in the state of the Void where the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower does not manifest, where there is the manifestation of the vision of pure consciousness alone, and where there is the manifestation of differentiation indicated by the internal unity residing within the objects of perception—[in that state, she resides].

And when the intensification of distinct differentiation occurs, those powers which have sequentially become Vyomacarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī are, in reality, according to the aforementioned method, non-distinct from the power whose nature is the Carcikā and Khecarī; thus, that supreme power of the Lord is one alone. As it has been said:
"His powers are this entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power."
[Thus attributed to the *Maṅgalaśāstra*].
Therefore, it is designated by means of the feminine gender.
For indeed, neither the differentiation nor the establishment of a distinction between the self, the mind, the sense faculties, and external objects is tenable.
Because it is devoid of intentionality and the like, and because it is non-manifest,
that very *khecarī* is perceived as being uneven through the forms of desire, anger, and so forth;
its equanimity, however, exists everywhere due to its nature as the perfectly full Bhairava.
Even the slightest lack of full knowledge regarding one's own unsurpassed nature constitutes the imbalance of the mental fluctuations;
this alone is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra),
because through the conceit of incompleteness, one brings about a state of limitation (aṇutva) within one's own self, which is the innate impurity (āṇavamala).

When there is a desire for the fulfillment of that incomplete form, the impurity called *māyā* arises from the perception of duality; furthermore, the impurity of action (*kārmamala*) manifests through the grasping of auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Upon the cessation of that inequality—which consists of the non-recognition of one's own true nature—the impurities cease to exist.
For mental states such as anger and delusion are indeed of the nature of the fully perfected consciousness of the Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka.
As it was said by the venerable Somānanda:
"That which possesses the nature of movement is Śiva. [Śivadṛṣṭi 3.94]
Thus:
"In pleasure, in pain, and in delusion, I abide as the supreme Śiva" (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.105).

Q: "Even in suffering, through expansion, by means of the application of fortitude for the sake of stability," and so forth. For the mental fluctuations such as anger and the rest—because they are identical with the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), and because otherwise their very acquisition of their own nature would be impossible—are indeed the divine goddesses who are the deities of the instruments (*karaṇadevatā*). Performing their various sports, they are the very form of the rays of the sun that is Śiva.

Likewise, those very [energies], having assumed innumerable forms through their mutual intermingling, are described in the scriptures of the Mata and other traditions as being worshipped as deities according to the distinctions of *kṛtyā* and so forth— manifesting in various gentle or fierce modes appropriate to specific rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*), killing (*māraṇa*), and pacification (*śānti*)— and they constitute the retinue of the venerable Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka. As it has been said:
Q: Beginning with "In the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), [the goddess] Kākavaktrā... [from the *Mataśāstra*?], it continues: Q:
"These very rays of the God of gods are the sustainers of the letters beginning with *ka*. [from the *Mataśāstra*?]

And so forth. However, when their true nature is not fully understood as such, they conceal the wonder of consciousness—which, even within conceptual thought, has non-conceptuality as its sole essence—by entering into a state of doubt and distress through various forms of conceptualization consisting of diverse clusters of syllables and letters, which are themselves of a most terrible nature. These [concepts], taking the form of deities, bestow the state of a bound animal (*paśu*) subject to the fetters of transmigratory existence. As it has been said:
Q: "The mistresses of the seats (pīṭheśvarīs), most terrible, delude [the practitioner] again and again," as stated in the *Timirodghāṭa* according to Kṣemarāja’s commentary on *Śivasūtra* 1.4.
Likewise:
Q: "They cause the subtle souls (aṇu) who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower," and so forth. Likewise...
Q: He who has become the object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds, having his power eclipsed by *kalā*, is known as a bound soul (*paśu*).
[Spandakārikā 3.13] Thus, when their true nature is known through the aforementioned reasoning, they bestow the state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā).
It has been said accordingly:
Q: But when it is firmly established in one place, then by restraining its dissolution and emergence, one attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara).

[Spandakārikā 3.19] Thus, the thorough knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpaparijñāna*) consists precisely in this: that even when a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) arises within these mental states (*vṛtti*), which at the moment of their emergence are of a single non-conceptual form, it does not— despite being colored by various sounds composed of collections of phonemes— become such [a conceptualized state].
He is joined with the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) consisting of a mass of phonemes (*varṇapuñja*),
which would fragment the essential nature of that subject who consists of conceptual thought (*vikalpātman*)— a nature that was previously characterized solely by non-conceptual activity.
Furthermore, conceptual thoughts are not distinct from direct experience (*anubhava*) or from other conceptual thoughts.
Rather, He alone is the Lord of the wheel of consciousness, who—through the coloring of existence differentiated by His own sovereignty—assumes various names such as "Being" and so forth.
Thus, liberation is indeed identity with the Khecarī;

and that is precisely the constant arising of the thorough knowledge of the nature of the Absolute (Anuttara), which consists in the ascent into the bliss of the twofold reflective awareness through the union of the Supreme Goddess with the Self of Śiva.

For Śiva consists of the emanation of the potency of the great mantra of supreme speech; he is joined with the emission of the Supreme Goddess, an emission that is replete with flowers whose essence is the density of that potency.

For indeed, whatever enters into all the internal and external organs abides in the realm of the central channel—which is the vital sap nourishing all the limbs—in the form of consciousness as the nature of *prāṇa*;
this is what is called *ojas*.

That very [consciousness], by virtue of being the vitalizing principle in all the limbs and thus possessing a nature whose potency is inseparable from them, further enters through the gates of the sense organs—such as the eyes and ears—in the form of an augmenting agent (*bṛṃhaka*), namely as visible forms, sounds, and so forth. Precisely because it is an augmenting agent, it awakens the fire of desire, which consists of the agitation of that potency.
As it has been said:

Q: Regarding the passage beginning with "from conversation, from the touch of the body," and so forth: by means of even a single object such as form (*rūpa*) or another, which is augmented by the intensified prior power, there arises the capacity to produce the agitation described as the "performance of all objects. Because everything is the essence of everything, agitation certainly occurs even through memory, conceptualization, and so on, by virtue of the nourishment of infinite sounds and other objects that consist of everything and reside within the mind.

Only the Great Virility (*mahāvīrya*), which consists of all things in their fully nourished state, brings about nourishment; neither that which is incomplete nor that which is diminished is suitable for childhood or old age.

And in the agitation of virility, even though it is non-different from its own nature as Virility, there arises the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting of the Great Emission (*mahāvisarga*) in the form of vibration characterized by space and time, which is the very essence of the perfect consciousness of Bhairava, consisting of the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*), and the ground of the easy birth of joy.

For even in the case of the eyes, form becomes a source of pleasure only through the process of being differentiated by that great emission (mahāvisarga), which consists in the agitation of its own power;

and in the case of the ears, [pleasure comes from] sweet song and the like. In other senses as well, another object attains only a state of complete manifestation by surging forth within its own self.
And likewise, for those whose vigor is not augmented by such [spiritual] energy, and who possess no intoxication consisting of the agitation of such vigor,
even the most beautiful form of a young woman, or the sweet, low-voiced singing emanating from the face of a shapely lady, does not culminate in complete bliss— just like stones.
To the extent that it does not become expansive, to that same extent it culminates in a limited aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
For where there is no wonder at all, there is merely insentience.
It is precisely the immersion in an exceeding wonder, consisting of the agitation of vital energy (*vīrya*), that is called "sensitivity" (*sahṛdayatā*).
Only for one whose heart is nourished by the ever-increasing power established through the habitual attachment to enjoyments does that extraordinary wonder arise;
even in suffering, this very person experiences such wonder.

For that which is situated within—the essence of power consisting of the happiness of beloved children and so forth—is indeed awakened through the perception of meditative cultivation, as well as through cries and other such expressions.

The essence of suffering (*duḥkhasattva*) consists of a specific wonder arising from the power of indifference—the realization that what was of a turbulent nature and had reached a state of expansion shall not come to be again. As it has been said:
"Even in suffering, by means of expansion... [Śivadṛṣṭi 5.9].

Thus, when—upon the complete filling of the winds and other elements within all the channels of the senses—one attains identity with the agitation of one's own power (*nija-śakti*) through entry into the great central *suṣumnā* state; and when, through the dissolution of duality on all sides, one enters the wonder consisting of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*) which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the full weight of one's own power;

and when, by entering the union with the *rudrayāmala*, which is the nature of the bliss of perfect emanation, there occurs the unfolding of the emission (*visarga*) that is the vitality (*vīrya*) of that Great Mantra; [then one attains liberation].
There is the manifestation of the state of Bhairava, which is characterized by the firm foundation [of the *dhruvapada*] and is free from the turbulence of waves.

For instance, at the time of trembling (*kampa*), even for that which consists of both genders in the form of the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*)— having gained its support through the strength of the vigor and enthusiasm of that [vital energy]— there is an internal bliss of touch consisting of the desire to emerge as the agitation of all vital energy,
which is witnessed by one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).
And this penetration does not consist merely in abiding within an imagined body; rather,

by means of the instruction on the direct realization (*abhijñāna*) of that [body], it is the entry into the form of the Supreme Goddess (*Parābhaṭṭārikā*), who is the creative sovereignty and bliss of the union of Śiva and Śakti— consisting of the Supreme Brahman— attained through the dissolution of the emission of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra-visarga*).
That will be explained [in the passage] beginning with "There, one should worship the emanation" (Parātriṃśikā 29),
and so forth; likewise:
Q: As in the passage beginning, "Just as [the tree] resides within the seed of the nyagrodha" (Parātriṃśikā 24), and likewise:
Q: "This is the Rudrayāmala" (Parātriṃśikā 35).
And so forth. It is also stated elsewhere:
"O Mistress of the Gods, by recollecting the fullness of a woman's pleasure through licking, churning, and striking, an overflowing flood of bliss occurs even in the absence of physical power."

[Vijñānabhairava 70] Thus, because it is remembered through *bharā* (intense longing), that touch—reflected within the channel (*nālikā*) of the central, non-artificial, supreme Self-power (*parātmaka-śakti*) in the field of that touch—even in the absence of the primary Śākta touch itself, becomes the cause of the agitation of the *vīrya* (vital potency) consisting of the internal Śākta touch; this is the intended meaning. Likewise...
Q: That bliss which concludes with the union of powers, their agitation, and the final immersion into power—that is the bliss of the reality of Brahman; it is called one's own innate bliss.
[Vijñānabhairava 69] Thus it is said.
Question: ... one should instruct [the disciple] in the Kaula [tradition] out of affection. [?]
And thus it was said by the Great Hero, the Blessed One Vyāsa: "My womb is the Great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs."
Thus it is also sung; and likewise by the venerable Somānanda in his own commentary:

Q: "The question concerns the Blessed Lady while she abides in *rata* (the state of bliss)," [as stated in the *Parātriṃśikāvivṛti* of Somānanda], "even though she is of the nature of the Supreme (*parā*) alone, with the intention of referring to the great intermediate space (*mahad-antarāla*) consisting of that.
Enough, then, with this extensive digression concerning the instruction on the secrets of the Trika scriptures.
This is the unsurpassed bestower of Kaulika-siddhi; by the mere knowledge of which, equality with the Khecarī is attained according to the stated method. [As it is said in Parātriṃśikā 2ab:
"O Lord, tell me this secret, the great secret."
It is "secret" (*guhya*) because it is not manifest;

for as long as there exists a cave consisting of the non-recognition of one's own true nature, [the reality] remains unmanifest even though it is present. And yet, it is "not secret" (*aguha*) on a grand scale, because it consists of such a wondrous power for everyone.

The Blessed Śuddhavidyā herself, characterized by the non-differentiation of the divisions consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, becomes the Triangle (trikoṇā) within Māyā when she assumes the apprehension of differentiation through an extraordinary reflection. Thus, even Māyā—the ground of the birth of the universe—is in reality Vidyā.

According to the principle stated, because she is fully known as being of such a nature, and because the three corners of the knower and so forth are concealed by the majesty of non-duality, she is called the "Great Cave" (mahāguhā).
And that very trident, in its true nature, is the locus of worship for the sake of the Trika. As it has been said:
"That Great Vidyā is the triangle, the Trika, the abode of all flavors;
it is indeed the state of emission (visarga). Therefore, one should fully worship the Trika."
Thus:
"In that way, a single light arises, pertaining to the means of knowledge, the object, and the knower.
(Siddhapāda? *Kramastotra* of Erakanātha)

Thus it is said. And so, within such a great cave—which consists of the heart of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which is the form of the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*), and which is the birthplace of the universe—there exists that which is "Maha" by way of its own self-revelatory wonder (*svacamatkāra*). This is the secret. For by this [secret], there is that sovereignty (*svātantrya*) which consists of the uninterrupted reflective awareness (*avimarśa*) of the light of Bhairava; and through the process of withdrawing its own nature from all objective entities (*bhāva*), it finds rest in the reflective awareness of the Self (*ātmavimarśa*).
For the "I" (aham) is the essence of the wonder of the power of the supreme mantra, which is the natural and unartificial state of Light. As it has been said:
"The repose of Light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva).
[Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi 22cd]

Thus [it is said]. That very thing is the secret, the supreme mystery. For indeed, Lord Bhairava—who, through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), rests in the form of the unmodified, unsurpassed, and eternal; who is the life-force of the entire web of creative powers (*kalā*); who is established as the beginning of all; and who is essentially beyond parts (*akalātmaka*)—he himself, assuming a form characterized by expansion, attains the state of emission (*visarga*). Of that very emission...

Because it consists of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) whose nature is the *kuṇḍalinī*, it again flows forth in the form of a human being as the *bindu*, which is the nature of the means of knowledge that is non-different from the expansion of that power.

Likewise, through the withdrawal of the three supreme powers— the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the trident (*triśūla*), and the root— there is always an entry into the supreme, unchanging state of the root, by means of the dissolution of its emission (*visarga*).
This will be clarified very soon.
In the previously mentioned Great [State] whose nature is supreme bliss, that which has been described by the aforementioned method as having the form of *a* is itself the secret;
and this alone is the great secret, the source of the birth of the world.
Likewise, through the bliss of both meditative attainments, [the state] is non-secret and consists entirely of wonder.
"O Lord" (*he prabho*) is an address to one whose nature is to manifest (*prabhavana-śīla*) such variety within one's very own self (*sva ātmani eva*).

This [is the meaning]: that [notion] which, with respect to the person being addressed (*āmantrya*), constitutes a state of identity and orientation toward the one being addressed (*āmantraka*), provides an additional meaning beyond the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). As it has been said:
"The meaning of the nominal stem is augmented by the vocative" (*saṃbodhanādhikaḥ prātipadikārthaḥ*).
[Cf. *Vākyapadīya* 3.7 (*Sādhanasamuddeśa*) 163 (+ Helārāja)].

Thus it has been determined by me alone in the *Śrīpūrvapañcikā*. Explain this: although it exists undivided as the nature of the Supreme Speech (*parāvāg*), join it on the level of the Visionary Speech (*paśyantī*) by means of the threading together of the sequence of sentence-connections, as was stated previously.

Q: Regarding the passage beginning with "abiding in the state of teacher and disciple" (*Svacchandatantra* 8.31a) and so forth, the identity of the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*) with the Visionary Consciousness (*paśyantī*) and the others has already been established previously. Likewise, that which is called *mahaḥ*—the secret of this state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*) which is connected to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) expressed by the word "mine" (*mama*)—is what is meant by "I" (*aham*).

For instance, that manifestation which occurs in the form "this is mine" has, as its further reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the singular essence of the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*). Furthermore, that "I-sense" functions by way of withdrawing all objective entities back into itself; thus, it is precisely of the nature of *mahaḥ*, as was stated previously. As it has been said:
"The fulfillment of this [object] conceived as 'this,' which possesses a fragmented reflective awareness..."
Q: That repose within one's own essential nature which consists of the reflective awareness "I am this" is *vimarśa*.
[From *Ajaḍaprāmātṛsiddhi* 15:
"Elsewhere also:
'The determination that "this is a jar" is not something distinct from name and form.'"
Q: The power of the Supreme Lord appears like the Self, and not as an "this-ness."
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Śrī Somānandapāda in his own commentary (*Nijavivṛti*) on the *Parātriṃśikā*:
"That which is seedless (*abīja*) is the nature of the pure Śiva."
And so forth; that very point has been elaborated by us.
Likewise, "one's own" (*svamama*) refers to that which is thoroughly non-existent as "mine.
Because it is rooted solely in the burden of the sense of "I," the universe does not possess for him even a trace of a sixth case-meaning (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*) characterized by a distinct designation.

Although for those who have been initiated into other systems—namely the *vijñānākalas* and the *pralayakevalins*—there is no sense of "mine" (*mama*) nor anything separate [from the Self], nevertheless, at the time of awakening, there must still exist a latent impression (*vāsanā*) capable of producing differentiation;
from the unfolding of that [impression], there arises the ascent of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*).
To remove that, the prefix *su-* is used in the sense of "thoroughly" (*suṣṭhu*).
As I myself said in my hymn:
"Foolish beings constantly fall into a state of wretchedness, thinking, 'Nothing whatsoever belongs to me';
whereas I have taken up the lofty burden, thinking, 'I am all that, and nothing whatsoever belongs to me.'"

Thus: by this auspicious knowledge—which is free from even a trace of the turbidity of the stain of duality and consists of the two-fold instruction on the ultimate truth—one does not measure [anything], because its nature is solely self-luminous.
It is "amā" (measureless) because it does not measure; it is "a-mā," where "a" means that "mā" (measure) is absent therein.
That Blessed Lady in whom neither "mā" (measure) nor its negation exists, and in whom there is no dissolution because she is eternally risen, is called "Amā."

*Amā* means "beautiful" or "ever-arisen. That *māyā* in which there is the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is such that it belongs to him (*mā*); thus, it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) ending in another possessive compound.

For the Supreme Lord, even within the conventional usage of means of knowledge and so forth, is composed entirely of supreme power (*paraśakti*), because he is in every respect of the nature of non-duality (*advaita*).
This is an address directed to himself.
This very point— the intended meaning of the infinite questions set forth in one and a half verses—
is now examined in order to determine that it has been stated here in summary form.
ParTri 2cd–3ab:
But that power which resides in the heart is Kaulinī, the mistress of the Kula.
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, so that I may attain satisfaction.
The heart, whose nature is consciousness, is the supreme foundation of everything—of blue, pleasure, and so forth, as well as of the body, the vital breath, the intellect, and the rest.
Its various cognitions of jars and other objects are merely the diverse manifestations of its own inherent freedom (*svātantrya*), through which it has fashioned these apparent distinctions.
Abiding therein is this power consisting of vibration (*sphuraṇa*), the mistress of the *kula*, who bestows the state of radiance upon the body, the vital breath, pleasure, and so forth;

she is the vitality of the circle of deities beginning with Brāhmī, the form of the very center of the entire circle of channels and sense organs, the pericarp that is the place of birth, and the essence of the *liṅga*.
And precisely there, within the *kula*, resides the Kaulikī, whose nature is the *kula*.
Alternatively, that which arises from *kula* and whose nature is *akula* is *kaula*;
she in whom that exists internally through identity is *kaulikī*.
For *kula* indeed becomes such only when it is established within the light of *akula*, as it has been said:
Q: But rather, "from the touch of the power of the Self" (Spandakārikā 1.8).
Likewise:
Q: Having taken hold of that power, the mantras, endowed with the power of the Omniscient One, proceed toward their respective functions, just like the sense organs of embodied beings.
[Spandakārikā 2.1] Thus:
"O Lord of the gods," such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest—this is an address.
The venerable Somānandapāda reads and explains it as: "Tell that to me" (*tan me kathaya*), and [he further glosses] "that" (*tat*) as "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Or rather, tell me that by which I may attain a satisfaction consisting of supreme bliss, becoming one with the essence of the freedom of the ultimate non-dual liberation; such is the connection [of the words].
There is also a reading "I go" (*vrajāmi*). By the word "I" (*aham*), that which is the very life of all subjects is constantly being pointed out.

And it has already been demonstrated previously that, by recognizing one's own nature as the Lord through such instruction on the nature of what has been taught, one attains satisfaction consisting of a state of fullness.
As it was stated by the venerable Somānanda in his own commentary (*Q*:
"Knowledge is the movement toward the Heart" [in the *Parātriṃśikāvivṛti*]):
And so forth.

For those whose minds constantly thirst to drink the nectar of Śiva— in whom existence has been established by Śiva for the destruction of all that is inauspicious— Abhinavagupta has forcefully composed this commentary on the *Praśna*, which pertains to the reality of the Trika, in order to tear asunder the knot in the sky of their hearts.
Thus, regarding this *Praśnasarvasva*, in the *Parātrīṃśikā*: Śrī Bhairava said:
This has already been explained;
what is the point of repeating it?
Bhairava is of the nature of sustaining and consists of the sound of the Great Mantra.
Only here has it been stated that the predominance of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) takes the form of "Maha" as the nature of withdrawal; this will become clear further on.
Therefore, this is the intended meaning here:
the supreme Goddess, Consciousness, as She unfolds from Her own essential nature...
It is called the power of the will, which is non-different from Bhairava.
Because its nature is to expand, it possesses the form of the power of knowledge and so forth,
assuming the bodies of Parā, Parāparā, Aparā, Paśyantī, and the others.
O Goddess, that very act of reflecting upon the nature of the expansion's form is called "the question," for you are the one who poses questions consisting of that very essence.
That very non-reflection upon the nature of its expansion is declared to be the supreme [instruction], which takes the form of a question and answer concerning it.
Starting again from that very point of non-recognition of the other, one repeatedly effects the withdrawal into the dense bliss of supreme consciousness, moving ever further inward.
The form of Bhairava, in which every expansion is entirely contained within,
perpetually unfolds itself in the very nature of the respondent.
Since these two— emanation and withdrawal— are not limited by time, this reality, consisting of question and answer, is indeed of a single nature.
Thus, the Gurus previously described that very essence of the entirety of the *Ṣaḍardha*, which is endowed with the unsurpassed connection to the Supreme (*para*).
Listen, O Goddess of great fortune, to that which is even higher than the highest.
This Kaulika rite which abides in the sky of my heart, I shall explain without doubt; it bestows the immediate attainment of the Kaula state. (Parātrīśikā 4)

"O Goddess" (*devi*) is as explained previously. She whose "great portion" (*mahābhāga*) exists— that is, she who, when cultivated through the practice of the teachings already stated and those yet to be stated, becomes the bestower of the great power known as supreme sovereignty—
she whose portion or part is Śiva, the Anāśrita (the Unsupported), who is renowned for his form as the Great Absolute (*paramamahat*).
For the power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*) contains within its womb the infinite thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and so forth.

"The Great One" (*mahān*) refers to that specific principle consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, which is a "portion" (*bhāga*) or "division" (*vibhāga*), a form dependent upon the limited powers (*kalā*).

Indeed, the power of the Supreme Lord, which is a single compact mass of consciousness (*saṃvid-ekaghana-śakti*), is called "the intellect" (*buddhi*) when it serves as the locus for the objects of knowledge and effects that appear as differentiated by virtue of its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
As it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānanda:
"...in the state of the other."
Q: "That intellect which is again subtle, omnipresent, and established [everywhere];
the knowledge consisting of awakening belongs eternally to that Śiva as his innate nature" (Śivadṛṣṭi 1.26–27).
Thus, the word *bhāga*—ending with the possessive suffix *-ka* (*matvarthīya*) meaning "that in which there is division"—denotes a divided form.

And since a delimitation within a differentiated body occurs only through mutual exclusion, the ascertainment of an object consisting of clarity, as it arises in the intellect, does so without even touching those entities existing throughout the universe— such as the pleasant and the unpleasant— but rather by excluding them.
Because the cognition of the mode of happiness consists of the nature of sovereignty over the *dharmas* and so forth, it is proclaimed as the outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) of the quality of *sattva*.

However, if one penetrates even that to its innermost depth, then by means of that very gateway, there would indeed be a constant arising within the abode of supreme bliss situated at the root of that [happiness].

Therefore, the "parts" (*aṃśāḥ*) of the Great One (*mahas*)—which consists of the bliss of the universe characterized by an unbroken, perfectly full, unrestrained, and independent autonomy—are portions characterized by happiness.

For whatever pleasure there may be, it has indeed attained a certain degree of form by being perceived as such through its entry into the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), which is the supreme abode of great bliss and liberation.
As it was said by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa:
"Whatever joy whatsoever is seen here, even throughout the three worlds..."

Q: "I bow to that God, the ocean of bliss, who possesses that *bindu*. According to the aforementioned principle, she whose form is that very thing called *maha*—which is to be worshipped—is the Supreme Lord’s own Śākta body, which is the "I" (*aham*) augmented by His own creative wonder (*camatkāra*).
And that very form is called the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā).

For this very reason, she alone, the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī), hears everything. Abiding by means of her existence known as "hearing," she possesses the sovereignty termed "synthesis" and "recollection"—which consists in bringing about identity with the mass of phonemes composed of her own successive and manifest vibrations within the cavity of the ears.
Therefore, even while hearing a specific sound submerged within a tumultuous noise, the cognizer behaves as if he does not hear it;
however, because the synthesis has the tumult itself as its sole object, the conventional usage occurs that "it was heard right there.

In reality, however, that tumultuous sound, upon entering the auditory space and thereby causing the phonemes to enter, becomes such [a synthesis], since apart from those phonemes, no distinct entity called "tumult" exists at all.
Furthermore, if one intends to express a specific distinction among those phonemes, the clamor would simply not arise due to the absence of a cause for it;
for even if it were the effect of a sound consisting of distinct phonemes produced by that intention, the production of a sound belonging to the same genus would still be logically possible.
In every respect, those very phonemes, when they reach a state of integration through that manifest form, are designated by the term "cacophony" (*kalakala*).
For one who is intent upon attending to that integration, there will certainly be a perception of some degree of clarity; thus, integration alone is what is useful here.
And it is that very same Blessed One, the Supreme Goddess Parā, who performs this integration. As it has been said:
Q: "Having ascended that power, the mantras... (*Spandakārikā* 2.10), and so forth.
For in reality, hearing, seeing, speaking, grasping, and so on, are the very form of the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī). As it has been said:
"By whom form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and sexual union [are perceived]..."
By this very [means] one cognizes; what remains here?
Thus it is stated by the Supreme Lord in the Vedānta;
however, "hearing" (śravaṇa) does not merely mean the auditory perception of phonemes in their distinct, clear, or even indistinct and faltering forms.
For indeed, the venerable Parameśvara himself has described this very point in the *Śrī-svacchanda-śāstra* at the occasion of determining the divisions of recitation (*japa*):
"That which is heard by oneself alone is known as *upāṃśu*.
[SvaTa 2.146] For here, regarding the state of the *madhyamā* [speech], it is stated that one hears it for oneself alone, and not another.

When there is clarity in the effort of the articulatory places (*sthāna*) and so forth, due to the conjunction and disjunction of the teeth, lips, and other parts, even if the utterance of the sound is extremely subtle, it would be heard by those standing very close; thus, the consequence is that it becomes "with sound" (*saśabda*). "That which is heard by others is proclaimed to be 'with sound' (*saśabda*). (SvaTa 2.247)

Thus it has been said: "And here there is no distinction such as 'near' and so forth. However, when there is a conjunction of the lips, palate, and other organs within the range of perception belonging solely to another subject, even if the hearing belongs only to oneself and not to the other, this nevertheless becomes the *madhyamā* state, because the phoneme does not acquire an external self-nature.
For [the sound] is indeed produced as a distinct phoneme due to the impact of the breath;
yet in that case, the impact of the breath would not extend to the point of external emission.
Furthermore, the movement of the lips and other organs would not enter into the constituent part of the phoneme, but rather it would be restricted to itself for that moment.

Even when there is a conjunction of efforts involving clearly articulated places of articulation (*sthāna*) and modes of formation (*karaṇa*), which serve as the basis for the simultaneous operations of bodily gestures, winking, and hand movements during the production of phonemes (*varṇa*), if indeed there were a distinction between high and low pitch (*tāra-mandra*) among the sounds (*dhvani*) according to their degree of intensity,
resulting in hearing them from far or near, this would still in every respect be the domain of *vaikharī* speech, since it is heard by others; enough of this digression.
That very Supreme Goddess, through the application of address, is clearly spoken of as being of the nature of Śakti;
for all this universe consists of the triad of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, and is thus essentially threefold in form.

In that context, that which exists solely within its own self is purely characterized by insentience (*jaḍa*) and is primarily of the nature of "the other" (*nara*), as in the expression "the jar remains.
This very [state] is the object of the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*), known as *śeṣa* (the remainder).

On the other hand, that which appears even as "this," being addressed as such, wherein the state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*)—distinct from the self—is concealed by the state of the "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) through the act of addressing, and which is designated by the word "you" (*yuṣmad*), is the form of Power (*śākta*).
"You stand.
For here, this very meaning of the word *yuṣmad* (you) and the reality of address consists in this:
"Just as I stand, so too does he"; thus, even for him, there is the freedom (*svātantrya*) of the wonder of the sense of "I" as delimited by the form of "we."
Identifying himself through the uninterrupted wonder of "I," he addresses [the subject] and designates it by means of the second person, which refers to the object "you.
For this is the Goddess Parāparā.

Furthermore, when there is the self-reflection of "I" characterized by absolute freedom that is entirely independent of the uninterrupted wonder, and wherein one thinks "I remain," that is the emergence of the Supreme Lady (Parābhaṭṭārikā), wherein the Person (puruṣa) possesses the state of excellence. As it has been said:
Since I have transcended the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Thus [it is said in Bhagavadgītā 15.18].
Here, by the word "I" (*aham*), which refers to the meaning of the pronoun *asmad*, it is stated that I am superior even to both the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*).

For in this context, the word "I" does not everywhere designate a limited entity such as the body and so forth, because such a thing would contradict its nature as perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Thus, such is this form, which consists of self-manifestation and is of the nature of Śiva.

For this very reason, there is neither any deficiency nor any excess in this consciousness, which consists of the manifestation of its own self-awareness; for that which is of the nature of non-luminosity cannot enter into that which is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*).

Furthermore, relative to that, even "mediocrity" (*mādhyasthya*) is nothing at all. Therefore, those [states] characterized by the uninterrupted nature of that consciousness have no power over what is established as the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is defined by the absence of any indication and stands as the locus of increase, decrease, and the middle.

The referents of "we" (asmadartha) [are not interrupted]; even when the referent of "you" (yuṣmadartha) is interrupted, it remains exactly so. For this very reason, "you" and "we" are said to be without gender (aliṅga).
The application of number is indeed justified through a metaphorical transfer based on the body, because it encompasses powers such as "the other" (para) and "the non-other" (apara).
For instance, one may contemplate an infinite number of bodies and so forth— which appear as differentiated by the freedom of one's own autonomy— as a single unity,
using such expressions as "we two," "you two," or "we" and "you."

However, the processes of accumulation (*upacaya*) and so forth pertaining to the body cannot even be metaphorically attributed [to consciousness], because it is impossible for that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) to undergo decrease or increase.
For everything consists of the essence of all things; thus, even insentient human beings, having abandoned their former forms, come to partake in the nature of Śākta-Śaiva reality.
Listen, O pressing-stones!
[cf. Mahābhāṣya 3.1.1;
cf. Vākyapadīya 3, Puruṣasamuddeśa 2]
For there is the recognition: "I am Meru among the peaked mountains" (Bhagavadgītā 10.23), and even "I, Caitra, speak.

That which is of the nature of the power (*śakti*)—that is, the referent of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad-artha*)—indeed assumes the nature of a person once it has abandoned its form as a mere power; for this is understood even through the non-addressive usage, such as "you, whose power of courage and fearlessness has departed."

Because there exists a perception through such [terms] as "you" (*bhavān*), and through specific cognitions such as "the feet are heavy," which have as their object the first person consisting of a human being appropriate for another state;

and because even for one who has abandoned the form of *śakti*, there would be the nature of Śiva in the form of "I" (*ahaṃ*), since there is the cognition: "O friend, O beloved, I am indeed the very essence of body and mind."
Even though its nature is Śiva, it indeed enters a body consisting of the individual soul (nara) and power (śakti), as if its conscious nature were abandoned—
thinking, "Who am I?", "This is I," or "Oh, I!"
For in expressions such as "Fie on me! or "Alas for me!", the term "I" refers to an uninterrupted autonomy that has been made subordinate;
whereas primarily, it is the interrupted state of "this-ness" (idantā) that is perceived, wherein the emergence of the goddess Aparā occurs.
In expressions such as "I am he" (*he 'ham*), there is indeed the touch of the supreme and subordinate *śākta* vibration (*spanda*) of Śiva;
however, each preceding stage is invariably present within the subsequent one.
Therefore, by means of a clearly manifest realization of the human form (*nararūpa*), one is certainly able to ascend to the heights of the *śākta* and *śāmbhava* states.
Furthermore, this ascent does not consist of a clear cognition through inversion;

rather, because each of these three groups possesses a triple nature by virtue of not abandoning its own respective form, it partakes of the forms of one, two, or many. For it has been said in the *Q*:
"A single reality becomes twofold, and being twofold, it becomes manifold."
[Kulapañcāśikā 3.2ab] Thus:

for when there is a single nature (*ekātmakatva*), because there is no counter-correlate (*apratiyogitva*), there is the state of Śiva; when a counter-correlate is possible, there is the state of Śakti. In multiplicity, there is indeed duality, which is the human nature (*narātmabhāva*) of that very One alone. For even in the cases of "a jar," "a jar and a cloth," "jars," and "a jar, a cloth, and a stone," as well as "he stands," "they two stand," and "they stand," this is merely the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) through unity itself. As it has been said:
Q: "Having made the manifold one, who would not be released from bondage? (as in Kulapañcāśikā 3.2cd).

For this very reason, when there is a simultaneous reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of Man, Śakti, and Śiva as one, there is indeed an entry into each subsequent essential nature, because that alone is in reality their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The very sequence of cognition—"he and you both exist," "he, you, and I all exist"—is followed by grammarians through their rules of refinement (*saṃskāra*), the essence of which is uncreated.

And so it is even with words in one's own vernacular; even in those of the Buddhists, the Andhras, the Draviḍas, and others, where not even the name of refinement remains, this same sequential order of expression prevails.

Furthermore, the sequence of words, by following from its very root the realization within the heart (*hārdī pratītiḥ*), would lead one to understand that because that realization consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the realization itself is likewise of such a nature.
As I have stated:
"Speech that does not reach the heart is no speech at all."
Thus, this cognition is in every respect uncreated (*akṛtakā*). As it has been stated in the *Q*:
"Without them, there would be neither word, nor object, nor the movement of consciousness.
And also in the *Śrīmālinītantra*:
Q: Thus, having taken as the basis the entire aggregate of atoms, just as they exist, so have you described the power of Śambhu, which is the one and only power of Śaṅkara.
Thus it is said in the *Mālinīvijayottara* (3.34). Also, in the *Śrītantrasamuccaya*:
"This entire universe always exists as permeated by Nara, Śakti, and Śiva."
Q: In legal proceedings, [the testimony] of worms and that of the omniscient ones are in every respect equal.

Thus, that very [reality] consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva has been demonstrated through the instruction of the tradition of clear realization. therefore, enough of this [discussion] which captivates the hearts of only a few fortunate and learned people who have been purified by the descent of supreme grace and possess the heart of the tradition.
This has been explained by way of digression;

Regarding what was stated as "the response to the response," how is it that this is not a response? To that, the reply is: that which is not a response even to a proximate response follows the sequence previously explained.

Therefore, disregarding even the answer—[the genitive case here is used] in the sense of disregard (anādare ṣaṣṭhī)—Q: [the question arises].
For the subsequent form (*uttara-rūpa*), having disregarded its own state, is indeed the unsurpassed form (*anuttara-rūpa*).
This distinction of the subsequent form exists only by resting upon the ground of non-difference; as it has been said:
"Even the establishment of another [as self] occurs for another only so long as the other has not been made one's own."
Q: That cannot be done, because the Buddha is supreme, supreme.
Thus,
likewise, this [teaching] is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) even for the subsequent portion of the text, as it cannot be surpassed by that either.

The unsurpassed place of rest for the "Northern" [practice], which consists of the impelling of the trident and so forth—what is that? He says: from which this Kaulika procedure arises.

"Kaulika" means having the nature of *kula* and *akula*, as explained previously. As it was said [in the *Q*]: "Since everything..."— for indeed, this entire universe, consisting of consciousness, mind, vital breath, body, pleasure, pain, the senses, the elements, jars, and so forth, exists as non-different from the single, supreme, sovereign Bhairava-consciousness, whose nature is pure awareness.
It abides in its form;
for although the form whose essence is awakening never sets— since if it were to set, it would follow that it could not manifest at all—
nevertheless, the delimitation consisting of mutual exclusion does not exist therein.
All entities are indeed the universal self;

and if they were not established therein, then even the initial synthesis and so forth would not serve to impel the senses. Thus, the entire collection of entities is non-different from the reflective awareness of "I" alone, which is appropriately free from the emergence of "this-ness."
It remains free from the conceptualization of division;
therein there is no limitation whatsoever.
Thus, wherever this Kaula method is clearly manifest, it stands as established and has attained rest.

For all this [universe], consisting of thirty-six principles, though created by its own power from Śiva—who is the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), whose nature is the consciousness of universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*), and who is primarily characterized by supreme power—nevertheless comes to rest within that very same self-nature which is primarily characterized by power and consists of the specific vibration (*viśeṣaspanda*) of Bhairava.
That alone is the state of things being established in their own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*). As it has been said:

Q: Regarding the phrase "in which all [exists]": this very reality, whose nature is Śiva and Śakti, consists of both the universal and the particular; though it is of a single essence, it is differentiated by the Supreme Lord himself for the sake of providing a means of instruction and entry.
When analyzed, however, it is in fact one alone—the independent, conscious "I" (aham), the unsurpassed (anuttara) whose essence is the power of sovereignty.
In what kind of own-nature does he abide?
[Answer: In the sky of my heart.

For, ultimately, among all things from blue and so forth down to a mere worm, there is not even the slightest form such as "blue" that does not rest within a portion of consciousness; rather, it is the perceiver alone who [possesses] the state of being mounted upon a portion of uninterrupted wonder, [expressed as] "mine."

That very [reality] has been purified by us through reasoning, instruction, and refinement, and made to enter the heart;

And that very Supreme Lord, whose nature is Bhairava, who has been described as the unsurpassed, eternal abode of the *ākula*, is this very reality—this entire existent world—which consists of the Kaulika ritual.

This is because even those factors proposed by others as the grounds for existence—such as connection with "Being" (*sattā*), causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and so forth—are untenable as causes of existence; for if they themselves lack existence, it is impossible for them to function as such. From the very beginning, existence (*sattva*) consists precisely in that light whose life is such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);

Alternatively, it is so called because, while existing as the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*), it exerts effort (*yatna*)—that is, it acts—since its vital breath is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
The form *tat sadyaḥ* is a neuter designation used with the suffix *kvip*;

This has been stated in the *Śrīsiddhasantāna*:

Thus it has been said:

and which causes the lotus of the heart to blossom for those purified by the teaching of the Trika (the *Ṣaḍardha*).
The radiant sun of this commentary, which possesses a gentle luster that dissolves the vast flood of the bonds of contraction and the infinite, has been illuminated by Abhinavagupta.

Thus, it has been stated that the Kaulika method is that from which it originates, that upon which it rests, and that of which this Kaulika reality consists; that very thing is the Absolute (Anuttara).

In this regard, what indeed is the Kaulika procedure, how does its expansion proceed from the Anuttara, how is it established in this very [Anuttara], and how is it of a single form with the Anuttara? Desiring to determine all that— including the statement "the Anuttara even of the Uttara"— by expanding upon it for disciples who have attained proficiency in discernment through the realization of the reality extracted from reasoning,
scripture, and self-verification, the Blessed One introduces another work.

But for those whose subtle latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the conceptual construction of the conceit of duality have been utterly crushed by such firm instruction, everything is accomplished by this alone—
namely, by the question concluded in the pair of verses beginning with "How is it unsurpassed? and so forth.

By means of the subsequent half-verse beginning with "Listen, O Goddess," which has been determined [in the text], the state of having accomplished all that was to be done belongs to those who have attained the status of a *jīvanmukta* through immersion in the realization of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) state.
Therefore, we proclaim with uplifted arms that one should find rest in this alone, by being purified through firm conviction.

Thus it has been said that one enters another text for the sake of discerning the Kaulika state situated within the stainless mirror of the supreme, unsurpassed state of Bhairava. As it is stated in ParTri 59ab:
"Now, all the initial lunar days (tithis) are the vowels ending with the bindu."
Within that, by the conjunction of time, the Moon and the Sun are proclaimed.

There is a quartet of concentrations (dhāraṇās) on air, fire, water, and Indra;
above that is the well-known group beginning with Śa, and before that is the pentad of Brahmā.
