Nor does this lead to an infinite regress, for even knowledge and will possess the nature of further expansion and non-expansion, and so forth.

It must be stated that for those two—expansion and non-expansion as well—there would follow the undesirable consequence of further conceptualizing internal expansions and non-expansions of will and knowledge, and so forth.
For now, cease this wandering in the delusions of external confusion;
enter rather the subtle path of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

For as long as consciousness arises even with respect to a jar or similar object, for that very duration the knowledge itself manifests, its self-revelation variegated by the aspect of the knowable jar and so forth.

And in that case too, regarding the state of being variegated by those forms, even the subtle initial emergence of the manifestation of the jar and so forth is perceptible, because the non-existence of anything else is manifested through the arising of that single entity.
The sovereignty of consciousness itself—consisting of the desire for an entity to emerge—is indeed obtained through the means of valid cognition that is one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).
The consciousness that consists of the non-accumulation of those states—dense, full, and the very existence of absolute freedom—is itself perceivable.
Being a mass of bliss within one's own self, one should likewise be autonomous; thus, even bliss is not to be denied.
And the Supreme Lord Bhairava, the possessor of power, whose essence is the ineffable, supreme wonder, shines everywhere as the agent.

Even there, however, when one reflects upon the essential nature of the Unsurpassed Bliss (anuttarānanda), the Will (icchā), the Lord (īśana), the Opening (unmeṣaṇa), and the Non-closing (unmeṣa), those very powers of consciousness— the Blessed Goddesses— descend as nothing other than consciousness itself for those who rest upon the plane of knowledge by investigating their continuity.

This is because they are non-different due to their fullness, since differentiation arises only from the limiting adjunct of the object of cognition, and that [adjunct] exists merely as something cognized within the body.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrītantrasāra* that "the reality is the shadow of one's own head": "Just as when one attempts to step over the shadow of one's own head with one's feet, the head cannot be located at the place of the feet; so too is this *baindavī* digit."
Thus, this group of six has been set forth, ending with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
Now, the unfolding of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is investigated.

Action is that which consists essentially of the intensity (*saṃrambha*) in assuming a sequential nature—a wonder consisting of the manifold intermingling of the mutual essences of will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) themselves.

In this regard, whatever undergoes a state of confusion through being mixed with another due to a connection with that other, it becomes so by way of first being overtaken by a nature that is essentially empty and beyond conceptualization (*anāmarśanīya*), just as a frog and the like [are swallowed] by water-birds.
In that process, its body consisting of the unsurpassed bliss (*anuttarānanda*) does not depart.

Because its nature is inexpressible, and because it serves as the ultimate foundation for all cognitions by existing as the substratum of everything, it is not merely that; rather, due to its capacity for succession, the *saṃrambha* (impulse) is indeed *icchā* (will), which extends up to *īśanā* (sovereignty) and is capable of unfolding within itself in the state of supreme bliss (*anuttarānanda*).
Thence, plunging into its own void-like body, that very [impulse] first enters its radiant, luminous form, as if consisting of light, [expressed as] "ṛ ḥ".
For here, how could the following of "i" and "ī," as well as the audible presence of the repha (r) in its radiant form, be denied?
As the venerable Puṣpadanta has said:
Q: Or rather, it is established through the commonality of phonetic similarity (*raśruti-sāmānya*).
For when one desires to enter into a void and motionless form, the ascent of the ladder of the perception of luminous form is already established.
Consequently, following the phonetic similarity of *la*, which consists of the stability of the true nature of the earthly form due to the entry into that motionless form, there arise *ḷ* and *ḹ*.

And thus, at the limit, by transcending the essential nature of the totality of all states, the very form of Īśana itself, having leaped for a longer duration, attains a motionless and void existence; it thus attains the state of *pluta* (the protracted vowel), according to the rule that "there are no long vowels for the sound *ḷ*.
For *a* and the other vowels, however, the state of *pluta* consists in the further prolongation of the long vowel itself.
And since that length is already established by the aforementioned rule and need not be sought separately, let it be for now.

This tetrad is said to be of a neuter nature (*ṣaṇḍharūpa*) because, through its entry into the state of emptiness, it is like a burnt seed; however, this is not because of an absolute absence of the nature of a seed, for there exists nothing whatsoever that transcends both Śiva and Śakti, who consist of the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*).
Because it is not mentioned in the Śrīpūrvatantra and other scriptures,
and because in worldly pleasures and the like, such a state of rest is of the nature of bliss, that very thing is called the "fourfold seed-syllable of nectar.
Thus, will and mastery [are established] within the body of bliss.

And having entered into the unsurpassed supreme abode— which exists from of old and does not deviate from its own nature— one pronounces "a ā i ī iti e," and not in the reverse order, as it is stated: "a-varṇa [becomes] e before i-varṇa."
Furthermore, there may be a distinction between entering [the state] and entering the unsurpassed state (*anuttarapada*).
For while there is clarity in entering the state of bliss (*ānandapada*),
there is subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*) in the merging with the unsurpassed abode (*anuttaradhāma*) when compared to that.
For thus the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Serpents, commanded:
"Among the Chandogas, the Sātyamugris and the Rāṇāyanīyas study [the word] as half 'e' and half 'o'.
Furthermore, even in the world, such extensive usage is clearly evident in the common vernaculars and regional dialects.

Even within the *Pārameśvara* [Tantras], that shortness observed in the letters *e* and *o* in relation to the long *e* and *o* during the application of limbs (*aṅga*), faces (*vaktra*), and so forth, should be understood in this very way, with the intention of half-*e* and half-*o*. Thus, the seed-syllable "e" is established.
This too, being thus variegated as the body of consciousness (*saṃvidvapus*), abides in that very same form as "ai," namely "a ā e."
The same should be stated regarding *unmeṣa* (the opening): "a ā u ū" becomes "o";

"a ā o" becomes "au". Although the unfolding (*unmeṣa*), which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), may plunge into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as it expands, nevertheless, its very entry into the dual form consisting of will (*icchā*) and sovereignty (*īśana*) is itself emptiness.

However, in the case of *icchā* (will) and *īśana* (lordship), there is no form consisting of their own transformation; thus, their status remains exactly as previously stated. Likewise, when *icchā* and *jñāna* (knowledge) have attained fullness through entry into the nature of the Absolute (*anuttara*), they subsequently relinquish that state of existence characterized by the vibration of such limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Then, by means of a body consisting of nothing more than the *bindu*—which is the realization of the true essence of the Puruṣa-tattva, which is consciousness itself and ascends to the state of non-dual existence—they merge into the Absolute state as "aṃ."

For indeed, the vibration of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is fully completed within the letter *au* alone; thus, because will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are included right here, its nature as a trident (*triśūla*) is described in the *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra* in such enumerations as:
"The fourth [vowel] by means of the trident," and so forth.

The *bindu*, moreover, is the state in which everything remains as nothing but sensation (*vedanā*). When the Supreme Lord— firstly by virtue of his primary nature as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*)— releases the entire universe, which remains as mere sensation, so that it may merge into his own self, and releases it from his own self through its emanation, he alone is the Supreme Lord.

Now, however, because the emission of Śakti (*śāktavisarga*) is predominant, it is "aḥ. For when the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) has reached its full intensity up to the vowel *au*, this much [of the phonemes] has entered therein.

These are the initial, middle, and final portions of the vibration of the powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action, belonging to the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*), which is the true essence of the venerable Lord Bhairava.

Their nature is one of ever-increasing radiance as they intend to manifest; they are clearly characterized by yogis who have ascended to their respective stages through the most subtle and intensive contemplation;

and they are described in the *Svacchanda-tantra* and other procedural scriptures (*prakriyā-śāstra*) as having the form of the "awakened expansion" (*prabuddha-prasaraṇa*), the "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*), and so forth.
For this very reason, it is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Śivadṛṣṭi-śāstra*:
Q: [Salutation] to You, whose form consists of a nature filled with the weight of supreme bliss, and who, through direct experience, are the Supreme Self in whom the triad of powers is dissolved.
And so forth.
Question: Its power also has attained the state of universal form, like that of a lump of clay becoming a jar...
Having investigated up to this point:

"For that reality is indeed one; there is no excess beyond its enumeration," it has been determined that the very principle of Śiva (śivatattva) assumes the state of Bhairava by virtue of being filled with the wonder of the power of the expansion and vibration of infinite and diverse sovereignty. In that regard, this aforementioned sequence applies.
Even in the first chapter of the *Saṃpradāya*, it is said:
"When he remains absorbed in the experience of pure bliss of consciousness,
his will is of that same extent, his knowledge is of that same extent, and his action is indeed of that same extent."
Q: It exists through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the three extremely subtle powers;
it is of the nature of consciousness, supremely blissful, undivided, and eternally supreme.
Thus [it is said]. Likewise:
Q: ...he knows the jar up to its base.
Q: He knows the cognition; herein lies the destruction of sensation for one who is free from desire.
Q: Because there is an absence of orientation toward it [the object], its cessation occurs without liberation;
it does not engage with what is loathsome, nor does it perceive without consciousness (citi).
Thus it is said:
"Whatever one desires to know or to do, that action arises from desire;
for previously, its prior and posterior parts were merely conceptual constructs."
Q: [It is] the attainment of the manifestation of that action, its unfolding. Q: And Śiva never assumes grossness through the consequence of such manifestation.
And so forth. This has been made heart-felt precisely because it is endowed with reason and constitutes the very life-breath of the entire essence of the scriptures (*āgama*).

This Supreme Lord emits the universe, and that [universe], consisting of the forms from *ka* to *kṣa*, begins with the earth and ends with the power (*śakti*); this much is the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), which is celebrated as the "sixteenth digit" (*ṣoḍaśī kalā*).

Q: Regarding the statement, "In the Puruṣa of sixteen parts, they call that the immortal part," this is indeed neither a numerical calculation nor even a Vedāntic view, but rather belongs to Śiva alone. And it is the power of emission (visarga-śakti) itself, the Supreme Goddess, which is the seed of the ground of supreme bliss.

For in this way, the form of the letter *a* and so forth, having assumed the nature of the *yoni* through the process of condensation (*ghanatāpatti*), yet without falling away from its own essential nature, is said to be the "state of emission" (*visargapada*) as it merges into that very nature of the *yoni*. O Great Goddess, that place where this emission finds its rest is called the mouth of the Guru; it is called the wheel of power (*śakticakra*).
And so forth. The *ka*-group is the density of the vowel *a* alone, because it is produced in the throat (*kaṇṭhya*).
The *ca*-group is the density of the vowel *i*.
Because [the letter *u*] is palatal,
its substitute is the labial class (*pavarga*), because [the letter *au*] is labial.
The dental class [of consonants] corresponds to the vowel ṛ, because it is retroflex; the dental class corresponds to the vowel ḷ.
Because they are dental: *ya* and *śa* are at the end of the *ca*-group,
while *ra* and *ṣa* are at the end of the *ṭa*-group.
The letters *la* and *sa* belong to the *ta*-group;
the letter *va* also belongs to the *ta*- and *pa*-groups.
Even for consciousness—which is formless and pure awareness alone—solidity is nothing other than its very nature as the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
And that [expansion] arises according to the stated principle, by means of the sequence of the sixfold group of powers (*śakti-ṣaṭka*).
Therefore, the five [elements] multiplied by six become thirty; with the addition of the six [powers], they become thirty-six.
Thus, the very seed of Śiva, through its own sovereignty, becomes dense and, abiding in some form consisting of Śakti as a flower, is designated as the "womb" (yoni).

For that very flower—consisting of the three corners of the grasped, the grasping, and the grasper according to the previously mentioned method—is in reality the locus of procreation only when it is conjoined with the seed;
for it is precisely at that time that it possesses the nature of a flower.
At other times, however, such a designation occurs simply by virtue of its inherent fitness (*yogyatā*).
Thus, that very flower is the form of the *yoni* by way of its triangularity;

it is the triad of corners consisting of the manifest and differentiated forms of the moon, sun, and fire—creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—as well as the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* channels, and the mixture of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and so forth.
The venerable Bhairavī, the Goddess of the Supreme Lord, is designated as the *yoni* because she serves as the foundational womb (*yonisthāna*) for that form.
And so, in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, while investigating the *Khaṇḍacakra*, this very point has been taught with primary emphasis:
"Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā, whose nature is the bliss of the triangle."
Regarding Mahāmāyā: cf.
*RauSuSaṃ* 4:28cd: "Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā, the cause of all causes."

*Āgama Niśvāsaguhya* 7.253ab, etc. For this very reason, it is taught in the *Śrītrikatantrasāra* that the union of Śiva and Śakti—which is the singular, dense state of such seed-syllables and flowers—is to be worshipped by oneself, by means of one's own self:
"Through the absorption of Śiva and Śakti, [one becomes] whose essence is the density of Śiva and Śakti."
Q: One should worship the supreme Trika, which is the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Regarding the phrase "the essence of the three tantras" (*trikatantrasāra*):
although this condensation (*ghanībhāva*) becomes manifest in the form of *vaikharī*, it nevertheless resides primarily within the body of *parāvāk*, which is the self of all things.
In that regard, the specific distinction is that even the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs of production (*karaṇa*), and the throat and lips are themselves the self of all things.

For indeed, one might even speak thus internally, "I see," and the experience is perfectly clear; moreover, the distinction [between sounds] is caused solely by their position and so forth, because phonemes have hearing as their single life-force.
What need is there for more?
Even a child being instructed reflects internally upon the multitude of objects as having such-and-such a nature;
he may reflect through error or even through doubt,
yet he certainly experiences some form of determination.
And that [distinction] is produced solely by the reflection upon speech;

for this very reason, even the application of closure (*saṃvāra*), opening (*vivāra*), slight breath (*alpapraṇa*), great breath (*mahāpraṇa*), aspiration (*āśvāsana*), and emission (*anupradāna*) must likewise possess an internally corresponding nature,
otherwise there would be no possibility of differentiation among the similar places of articulation (*sthāna*).
The powers of making things disappear must indeed exist, for otherwise,
the variety of mental constructs such as "I hear," "I have heard," "I see," "I have seen," "I intend," and "I have intended" would be impossible.

Therefore, having observed this method, enter further and further within and cultivate that consciousness wherein there is the installation of the Lord of Phonemes (varṇabhaṭṭāraka)— whose essence is the great mantra of freedom consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that very same unified consciousness— within the abode of the throat, lips, and so forth, which are the single mass of the awakening that is the self-nature of all things;
for this is the place where the non-differentiation of the unity of consciousness resides.

If it is asked how there can be a distinction such as "this is the instrument" or "this is the phoneme," it is because of that very sovereignty [of consciousness] within its own self of that kind, such that [it appears as]: "this is a jar," "this is pleasure."
What effort, or how great, is required for that [consciousness] which manifests as "this is knowledge" and "I am the knower," through such a manifold and variegated manifestation?
For this very reason, all things— stones, trees, animals, humans, gods, Rudras, Kevalins, mantras, their lords, and even Maheśas— are but one.

The stage of the Supreme Goddess (parabhaṭṭārikābhūmi) exists as the very self of all things in the form of the Supreme Lord; thus, that which consists of the body of sound—whether manifest or unmanifest, distinct or indistinct, and so forth—as it is projected through the totality of her various locations and other attributes, is celebrated as the "potency" (vīrya) of mantra.
For instance, although that same sound arises from various different places in instruments such as the vīṇā, vipañcī, kacchapikā, and murajā, it is nevertheless said to have a single location.
The same should be stated regarding high (*tāra*), middle (*madhya*), and low (*mandra*) pitches, even though they possess identity with the phoneme (*varṇa*) that persists therein.

For this very reason, the same phoneme may manifest from different articulatory locations (*sthāna*) in certain living beings; for example, when the sounds *ka*, *ṭa*, and *ra* are uttered by crows, they are all perceived as being produced from the belly, the lips, the throat, and the palate.
Even if they are unmanifest, they are nonetheless only that many, because they are sounds, and because there is no sound that exceeds the *mātṛkā*.

It is also incorrect to claim that even an unmanifest sound exceeding the *mātṛkā* is not included because it is useless; for even a sound in the form of unmanifest phonemes—such as the roar of thunder or the sound of the ocean—undoubtedly possesses the capacity to cause pleasure or distress. What other intended utility could there be?

In the *Pārameśvara* as well, the nature of mantra is primarily established for the unmanifest sound (*avyaktadhvani*) alone, because it is stated that the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and so forth constitute the very essence of the pervasion of mantra. And therein it is said:
"The sound that has reached the *nirodhinī* [channel] becomes auspicious and inauspicious," and so on.
Because sounds such as those of bells and bronze, as well as the striking of the ears and so forth, are described in the instruction on *nāda*:
"Just as a horse neighs, and as a tamed [elephant] seems to run,

The very union with the plane of emission is the abiding state of the vowels *ā* and so forth, which consist of the powers of bliss, will, exertion, unfolding, their subsequent expansion, and the diversity of their activities.

And that [sense of 'I'], in reality, is the soul of all things according to the principle just established; thus, being permeated by the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*), it is of the very nature of Bhairava.

I bow with natural spontaneity to that Goddess, who is my own abiding self, whose nature is the manifestation of "I" through the fullness of its activity.

By this, it is established that the letter *a* alone is the first of all [letters].

Even in cases such as *harṣa*, *ghaṭa*, or *nīla*, where letters beginning with *ha* and others appear, there too there is simply an implication of infinite preceding and following letters of its own kind.

Therefore, with this very intention, in the section on Time (*kālādhikāra*) and elsewhere, the diverse emergences and dissolutions of the Mothers, Rudras, World-Guardians, Planets, Nāgas, and so forth— preceded by the rising of sixty and its multiples of years— are described within a single breath, or even within a sixteenth part of a breath.

Thus, since even the second [aspect], such as the movement of the breath, consists of these infinite diverse emergences and dissolutions, the reality that is the ultimate truth is in fact that which is untouched by time (*akālakalita*).

At most, this much may be said: that which is not to be determined by illusory mental constructs (māyīyādhyavasāya) produces the conceit of non-existence; however, in supreme consciousness (parasaṃvit), that very thing shines forth at that very moment.

For this very reason, within a single cognitive act (jñānakalanā), the presiding of the triad of deities—expressed through such teachings as "one sees one thing, while another is conceptualized"—is never absent from anywhere. Furthermore, all cognitions are in reality the ultimate "I," consisting essentially of reflective awareness (vimarśamaya).

Thus, it is established that this entire universe resides within Him; the Supreme Lord, filled with the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), is indeed the emission (*visarga*) itself, both emitting and swallowing [the world].
Having become solidified, He assumes the nature of the letter *ha*, and through the variety of infinite combinations, He also attains the form of the letter *kṣa*.
This very [emission] consists of the agitation of the phonemes appropriate for the union of the Śakti-yoni, which is of the nature of the messenger (dūtī).

By resorting to the state of the unstruck sound (anāhatanāda), this emission—consisting of the multitude of those infinite entities surging from the central Suṣumnā plane—becoming detached, enters into the abode of the eternal (dhruvadhāman), which is the unsurpassed state (anuttarapada); this has already been stated previously.

These forms, beginning with A and so forth, which possess stability within the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of their abiding in the sixteen *tuṭis* and so on, join together a single *tuṭi* through a division of half-and-half portions; thus, they extend even externally into the form of time consisting of fifteen days during both dissolution (*pralaya*) and emergence (*udaya*). Therefore, they are called lunar days (*tithis*) and digits (*kalās*). Furthermore, it is the sixteenth digit alone, whose nature is emission (*visarga*), that is described in the venerable *Vātūla* and other scriptures as the seventeenth digit when it is about to separate [from the cycle].

In this very way the production of phonemes is possible; otherwise, how could the wind, spreading sequentially through the dental, labial, guttural, palatal, and other phonemes, strike the palate after having struck the throat?

For these very sounds, which consist of *nāda* and indicate mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*)— such as those of compassion, the erotic, or tranquility— whether occurring in cries of lamentation, endearments, or hymns of praise,

manifest the mental state by attaining the form of accents, intonations, and the like; they do so because they reside in close proximity to consciousness, independent of convention, obstruction, or other such factors.

The meanings and dharmas, such as the *udātta* accent and others, have been taught because they themselves constitute the nature of the six musical notes (*ṣaḍja*, etc. which experience the fluctuations of the mind.

Rushing forward in a "I first, I first" manner, appearing in a non-sequential way, and by their very nature as mental constructs (*kalanā*), they bring forth the very transition of the sequence of cognition as the spatial dimension being indicated;

Whatever exists in the Bhairava Tantra, all of that is accomplished from this [source].

The Śākta [nature] consists of the essence of the universe—which is the form of Bhairava—determined by the scriptures and the logic demonstrated therein, and whose nature is the Supreme Goddess Parā and the Non-Supreme (Parāparā).
Its heart, its core, is the form of Śiva, embraced by the Supreme Sovereign, the venerable Goddess Parā.

By the word *Bhairava*, there is the form of power (*śakti*), which is the universal nature of the totality of all things. For every individual differentiation (*bheda*) of the Self, which consists of the human aspect (*nara*), this is the heart consisting of Śiva.
This is because, as was stated previously, without that supreme non-duality and without that [universal] nature of being the self of all, this very differentiation would be impossible.

"O fair-hipped one" (*susroṇi*) is the address. That which has been described as the heart in the form of the womb (*yoni*) located within the hips— beautiful even in its illusory nature, for it does not deviate from being composed of pure consciousness— that [heart] belongs to me, whose self is the totality of the multitude of subjects, from the Great Lord of all mantras down to the immobile beings.

"Ours"— referring to that which is appropriately designated as having fallen [into manifestation]— is Brahman, whose nature is Bhairava, consisting of fullness (*pūrṇatā*), a single mass of the power of bliss arising from the emission (*visarga*) characterized by the surging forth of the internal vitality (*vīrya*) of the universe; it is vast (*bṛhat*), pervasive, expanding, and expanded,
and not like the vision of Brahman accepted by the reciters of the Vedānta, which remains close to a doctrine of mere nihilism (*kevala-śūnyavāda*).
And this third [state] is of a single form, supreme Śiva, in relation to humans and the rest;
for this very reason, it is that very heart which is taught as the primary object of worship in these scriptures and here.

Even those whose heart—whose essence is the pervasion of such potency (vīrya)—has not yet entered [into it], by the mere practice of external conduct alone, have their bonds of animal-like restriction (pāśava-niyama) loosened, slackened, and utterly shattered through the power of the gradual process.
They themselves rest in the state of pervading this heart;
for the entry into this heart is not something to be constructed by verbal conceptualization, such as "I have entered into this heart" or "this is the supreme Goddess."

On the contrary, this has been explained at length through the search for the inner path of the heart; however: "The snares of the scriptures do not contract the heart, nor does this world defile consciousness.
May there be that state of fullness, whose form is perfected by the path of the true nature, wherein the weight of the surging dissolution [of duality] is complete."
As I myself stated in my hymn:
"For those whose minds have become exceedingly clear through the onset of devotion to the Blessed One,
this state clearly dwells within their hearts in an instant."
Thus, for this very reason, three goddesses are to be worshipped in the corners.

In the practice of union (*yāmala-yoga*), even for the heroes (*vīras*), [the bliss] arises from the friction of the *dūtīs*, who consist of the agitation of the senses of bliss and eternal bliss.

that which is this Brahman, whatever moving or unmoving [it may be], is, in relation to the impure, pure-impure, and pure creations, the third, consisting of the pure creation.
For this very reason, it is conjoined with the lords of the lunar days (*tithīśvara*) by virtue of being its heart, and with their endings, the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*.

Likewise, the third Brahman, joined with the fourteenth and endowed with the end of the Lord of the Tithis, becomes the nature of Bhairava through the leaping over (pluti) of the form of the full void.

Indeed, when the Will (icchā), accompanied by the power of its own inherent nature (īśana), ascends from the plane of the knowable to the state of the void (vyoma), it rests for a moment on the ground of slight manifestation and then suddenly enters the infinite, motionless realm of the void— which consists primarily of wood and stone—

wherein it is said of the yogins who have entered the great void of dreamless sleep devoid of objects of knowledge: *“O you who have entered the great void of dreamless sleep, free from all objects of knowledge!”*

16) This entire web of reality (*tattvajāla*), surging forth as the very self of Bhairava, is therefore the expanded Brahman consisting of emission (*visarga*) as it is projected outward.

And that which stands outside, having become one with the self of Bhairava through the removal of the poverty of differentiation (*bhedātmakavyavaccheda*), is "expanded" by attaining the state in which everything is the self of all; thus it is the "state of emission.
This has been determined through careful attention.
Thus, the pervasion by the seed-syllables (*bījavyāpti*) consisting of sixteen aspects has been described.
However, the pervasion by the womb-syllables (*yonivyāpti*) has already been explained for each individual letter;
it shall now be examined with a view toward their systematic classification.

It consists of a composite of four stages—the assumption of different bodies in childhood, youth, old age, and death—and is composed of the five elements; internally, it possesses a third aspect consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), which takes the form of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths through their nature of inhalation and exhalation, ending with the *tithīśa*;
and it is called *brahman* because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*) and its emptiness (*śūnya*).

And here, that which is the heart, whose essence is power (*śakti*), these [five] are all subjects designated as the external self, the embodied self, the subtle transportative self, the inner self, and the supreme self; they consist respectively of the body, the vital breath, the city-of-eight (*puryaṣṭaka*), the void, and the fourth power (*turyaśakti*), having attained their respective states through a gradual process of increasing density of the seed whose nature is consciousness.

This is the Heart, whose essence is Bhairava. Herein lies the means of entry: one should traverse all levels of the subject without limitation, together with the thirteen internal and external faculties along with their primordial nature (prakṛti).
Fourteen and forty, added together and doubled, make eighty;
the lunar days (tithis) are fifteen;
the lords (īśas) and Rudras are eleven.
The end-points are three times [this number]. Thus,

by means of the method of simultaneous immersion according to the tradition, one should contemplate the very existence of the body— which consists of the agitation (*kṣobha*), the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*), and the separation (*visleṣaṇa*) of the emission (*visarga*) made to vibrate through the expansion of the potency of the mantra in the form of the supreme Śakti’s pulsation, both gross and subtle, located in the hundred and twelve vital points (*marmans*)— as being the very form of Bhairava.
That which possesses the four states of sweet, astringent, bitter, and sour— such as wine, *surā*, and fermented liquors—
is a substance whose end is marked by the lords of the lunar days (*tithīśa*) and which consists of the two emissions (*visarga*).
It is endowed with that which resides within the interval between the two senses.
The third impurity is that which is denoted by the word *kusuma* (flower).
Ashes are the residue remaining from the burning of the fuel of the world, which is Brahman. Water is the nourishing substance whose nature is Bhairava and whose form is fullness.
And the heart, which resides within all the senses, possesses a dual nature consisting of both *rasa* (sap) and *āśaya* (receptacle).
These substances, as they are obtained, serve to dissolve the impurities of differentiation.

For instance, whatever exists—whether it be of an earthly, elemental, or illusory nature—that appears, even though it falls within the sphere of will, knowledge, or action, is threefold in form due to its universal nature; it is emitted into the supreme state of Śiva, and everything is emitted from the state of Śiva.
Thus, this very uninterrupted process is free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).

Even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), such as that concerning a woman, an enemy, and so forth, has been an agent of this [liberation] in the past, is an agent of this in the present, and will be an agent of this in the future;

thus, because it is connected to the three times, emission (*visarga*) is indeed the supreme non-dual reality. On the contrary, for those who are cursed by fate, it is always nothing other than the ground of Śiva consisting of liberation.
The great forest of the mountain of fear that is saṃsāra has come to pass.

From the water [arises] a mass of the submarine fire, matted with flickering flames; from the full moon [comes] the thunderbolt that shatters the abode of fear; and from conceptual construction, which is the path for the expansion of power, there arises the destruction of worldly existence. How wondrous, how truly wondrous is this that spreads forth from the frustration of a ruined destiny!

Just as forms such as the four-armed and three-eyed [deities], or the full and emaciated [forms], within the midst of shapes, and substances such as wine and spirits within the midst of material objects, forcibly seem to settle upon that very existence (*sattā*), just as written letters [settle] upon the ground of true phonemes.
Thus they possess the quality of excellence;
likewise, this phoneme stands at the head among all the phonemes.
For instance, the letter *sa*, being of the nature of the nectar of supreme bliss, shines forth while simultaneously encompassing the entire web of phonemes.

Whatever constitutes the ultimate nature of reality, bliss, perfection, existence, and so forth— characterized by the resonance of the *sītkāra*, the arousal [of the breath], the trembling of the penis, and the contraction and expansion of the supreme organ—
that alone is, in fact, the non-illusory, real form of reality and the rest. For instance,

those skilled in discerning the gestures of another's heart extract their desired meaning from the mere phoneme *ga* alone, even when it occurs at the beginning, middle, or end of infinite words such as *gagana*, *gavaya*, and *go*.
Because one enters into the locus of truth (*satyapada*) to that extent, each individual phoneme possesses its own real capacity to signify. As it has been said:
"Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is confusion; by performing *saṃyama* on their distinction, knowledge of the cries of all beings arises" (Yogasūtra 3.17).

Thus, for this very reason, these particles, case-endings, and so forth—which consist of single phonemes such as *a* and *ca*—even within the sphere of *māyā*, express meanings that, as it were, belong to the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). These meanings are absorbed into the state of the subject (*pramātṛpada*), are averse to objectivity (*idantā-parāṅmukha*), and are non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*). They signify things such as negations and conjunctions that are inseparable from the respective things being negated or conjoined.
This indeed is the view of the venerable Bhartṛhari, as he says: "Every word is distinct from its first member, and every word is also expectant [of others].
[Vākyapadīya 2.2]
Thus it is in the investigation of sentences;

By the word "sadyas" (immediately), the penetration of the state of "sat" (being) is also indicated;
he attains the state of being oriented toward that [Reality] and the predominance of its supreme nature.
But it is not like the form of animals; on the contrary, it conceals itself.
For this very reason, it lasts for only a moment (*muhūrta*); even though it is not limited by time, it is merely an unfolding (*unmeṣa*) in relation to the calculation of others.
He who remembers and contemplates binds together the explained multitude of mantras and mudrās, unifying them within his own self through non-duality.
Having performed the sealing (mudraṇa) on all sides—that is, everywhere—by means of the Śākta form which kisses and touches the universe;
the particle *tu* is used for emphasis.

Only he who is sealed by the vibration of Śakti (*śāktaspanda*) and thus contemplates the nature of Śiva as consisting of such reality acts in this way; not one who is merely a human being, such as a stone or the like.

Whatever is past, whatever is future, and whatever is of the nature of misfortune—since there was nothing else prior to it—he alone speaks of that and brings it to its conclusion through his volition (*saṃkalpa*). How? When asked "How?", "how" refers to a question (*praśna*), which is the desire to know; one who possesses such a question is described as "one who has asked."
Q: Whatever one indeed intends to know, that very thing, being internal, one brings forth externally.
As it has been said:
"Just as the Creator, when requested according to one's desire, brings about for embodied beings the objects situated in the heart of the waking state by causing the rising of the moon and the sun."

[Spandakārikā 3.1] and so forth. For this one [consciousness] remains exactly the same even during recollection, imagination, and the like; the past and the future do not exist [as such]. As it has been said:

Because its nature was already such that it lacked any superior form, and because it cannot tolerate limitations such as "it knows this" or "it does that," it possesses the quality of being manifest all at once (*sakṛdvibhātatva*).

For this very reason, it has been stated repeatedly that, since the present time lacks [the capacity for] past and future in relation to the reality of the object, the true essence of reality is indeed untouched by time (*akālakalita*).
That very [reality], however, manifests the manifold power of time.
Furthermore, even that which is considered a mere *ghaṭikā* (a unit of time) during the waking state—
in that very same [time], subjects who have entered into a dream experience its manifoldness;
they even perceive the variety of days, watches, years, and so forth.
According to this principle:

*pra* means excellent; *hara* means withdrawal, which is called *akula*. Immediately following that, the intended meaning is the devouring—that is, the consumption—of the form of the Deity’s will, which is expressed by the word *preta*, as it is directed toward the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) residing in the *sadāśiva-tattva*; [it is the devouring] of forms, of the *kalās*, of the eye, and of form together with the sense organs.
Having made oneself proceed continuously, one perceives—without doubt—what has been drawn in by the powers whose forms are obstruction and emission.

This is what is meant: that which is called "vision" belongs to the possessor of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), who is mounted upon the foundational reality (*sattā*) known as the subsidence of all waves [of manifestation], due to his union with infinite majesty and sovereignty.
That very will attains the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which consists in the appearance of a slight and indistinct differentiation of the object desired within itself.
The power of that knowledge is the external containment of all the senses, whose nature is particular vibration;
this alone is the continuous movement.
And that which is liquefaction is itself consumption.

These very [factors] apply to vomiting and eating as well, because perception consists of a single manifestation (*prathā*) in every respect, and because manifestation possesses such a variety of forms.
Furthermore, even the state of having an indeterminate object in both cases is undoubtedly present in instances such as a post or a person.
Thus, the power of the Supreme Lord consists of the nature of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*).
But in this way, He is Bhairava, the possessor of the power of memory whose form is both supreme and non-supreme; thus he says, "for two watches," and so forth.
Remembering in this manner, he becomes the void (*vyoma*) wherein [the self] exists within the *puryaṣṭaka* and the empty state, assuming the nature of that subject (*pramātṛ*).

When one repeatedly touches upon and even remembers that form called "vision" (*darśana*), which was previously characterized by the [time-unit] *prahara*, then—as before—the connection is: "he sees directly and without doubt, drawn forth by the powers of Rudra.
For it has been stated that even then, that too is indeed vision.

Thus, he is said to be "endowed with the power of conceptualization whose nature is other. When, while situated in the void (*vyoma*), seeing and remembering by means of the triad [of powers], he sees once again—then, by this triad of visions characterized by the watch-periods (*prahara*), the Mothers, who consist of the internal subject, are the powers of the Supreme Lord. And because they are the subject itself, they are established as independent of the establishment of objects for any other subject.

Through yoga characterized by identity with that very form, there is sovereignty; likewise, those rays of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which have grasped a portion of autonomy and possess strength— that is, an unimpeded range everywhere in comparison to the functions of the great external senses— are also indeed perfected (*siddha*).

Because their activity proceeds with impetuosity precisely through being independent of the constraints of the bonds (pāśa) and the seat (āsana) everywhere, the "heroes" (vīra)—namely those called the faculties of cognition and action—are indeed perfected beings (siddha).
Furthermore, their lords, whose nature consists of the phonemes beginning with *ka* (*kādi-varṇa*), are also perfected beings.

Moreover, the multitude of powers (śakti-samūha), which consists of the deities such as Brāhmī and others—arising from the extraction of those *kādi*-phonemes and characterized by the various mental fluctuations (citta-vṛtti) of aversion, passion, and so forth—is likewise indeed perfected.

Therefore, he is powerful. All these, acting together by the command of another, bestow upon that other person their own nature consisting of the conceit "I"— that is, the accomplishment whose essence is the conceptual construction "this one is the other"— or rather, they grant the very desired fruit which is "I."
This application of conceptual and non-conceptual [cognition] occurs respectively regarding the purposeful action that is not yet known and the purposeful action that is already known.
To say more:
even those mantra-practitioners who have attained mastery over the mantras of other families accomplish [their goals].

The sense is that without this, ultimate realization (pāramārthikī siddhi) does not occur.
[This refers to the passage beginning with] "Whatever [is done], O Bhairava," and so forth.

Likewise, those who have attained perfection, those who are attaining it, and those who will attain it through the yoga of *aṇimā* and the other powers— all of them do so by means of this very [heart-mantra].
Indeed, without entry into this heart, even mundane accomplishment (*siddhi*) is not possible.
Since whatever collection of accomplishments (*siddhi*) exists within the *Bhairava* Tantra, which is the soul of the universe and the totality of ritual action, arises from this very source;

thus, this Supreme Lord alone, whose essence is the Heart, is conceived as possessing a unity with infinite consciousness—constantly arising and being withdrawn—that is nourished by the triad of powers.
Being thus conceptualized, He [removes] the unseen, which is non-perception itself, the impurity of *māyā* consisting of nescience (*akhyāti*), the "scum" (*maṇḍa*).
And it destroys the essence of entities, which is called their differentiation.
Thus, this heart is unseen even by the cosmic egg;
there are indeed only four eggs.
*Lopa* means contraction (*saṃkoca*). That which is associated with it is [the state of being contracted].
Thus, this Supreme Lord, who consists of both *vidyā* and *māyā*, is one alone as a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), as it has been said:

then, the passage beginning with "when this [mantra] has been uttered" is to be explained quite clearly, because in matters of visible results, a sequence of actions dependent on necessity (*niyati*) necessarily requires a fixed ritual procedure.

Now, regarding this threefold subject matter, it has been said:

It defines that state of being unsurpassed, which is supreme among all things:

He shall always possess accomplishment; he is a yogi and he is the initiated one.
Even without seeing the mandala—the wheel of deities—and even without attaining union through the practices of *caryā*, *niśāṭana*, *haṭha*, and so forth;
and even without directly perceiving the mandalas in the form of the wheels and sub-wheels of the channels within the body through yogic practice;
that is, even without having seen the mandalas such as the triple-pronged trident and the lotus.
In this case, there is no need for initiation through a mandala or other such means.
Thus, someone who is graced by the descent of the supreme power (para-śaktipāta) knows: "This very knowledge is indeed initiation; what other initiation could there be?
For this very reason, one who knows thus is initiated by the all-pervasive Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka.
Therefore, the statement "and one who has taken the mantra by oneself" refers to mantras other than this *hṛdaya* (Heart-mantra);
for this [other] mantra is not the *hṛdaya*, because it transcends the forms of the Mantramahēśvaras and their respective Maheśvaras.
It has been determined that this Heart is indeed not to be written in books; its attainment occurs in reality only through the grace of the descent of the supreme power (*para-śaktipāta*).
Likewise, the phrase "anyone whatsoever" indicates independence from caste, vows, conduct, and so forth.
For here, direct realization alone is primary.

That yogi partakes in accomplishment because "they desire yoga as oneness" (MVT 4.00); and his initiation consists of the characteristics of bestowing knowledge, [bestowing] illusion, and [the removal of] karmic traces.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), and that [emphasis] should be understood as applying in every respect:
"That very one is the yogin who possesses accomplishment; he is the initiated one.
That is to say: he alone possesses accomplishment, he alone is a yogin, and he alone is the initiated one.
Regarding that, it says "eternal" (nityam).
ParTri 19ab states: "By the mere knowledge of this, [everything] is known through all the powers."
He is known by all the deities and all the powers who are omniscient; knowing this very fact,
whatever is known even by them is known by him merely through his own knowledge, as previously stated.
"In all powers" (*sarvābhiḥ śaktibhiḥ*) is the instrumental case used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*).
Likewise, [it is stated] in ParTri 19cd:
Indeed, even without yoga, one becomes a master of the Śākinī-kula.

By merely knowing this, even without the yoga of practice— which consists of attaining identity with that [Śakti] upon the falling away of the illusory body— one becomes the Lord of the Wheel of Śaktis (śakticakreśvara), possessing the nature of the universal vibration (sāmānyaspanda) of the Śākinī-kula, which is of the nature of Akula.
Moreover,
one who is ignorant of the rules becomes a knower of the rules with respect to the performance of sacrifice. (ParTṛ 20)
Ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is action (*kriyā*), and knowledge (*jña*) is wisdom (*jñāna*).
He who lacks these two is a bound soul (*paśu*),
as it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:

[Kiraṇa 1.15] Thus, even though he is a bound soul, by the mere knowledge of this [teaching], he becomes an agent and a knower with respect to the performance of ritual injunctions and the cognition of objects, as one who possesses both.
And its sacrifice, even if incomplete, becomes complete because the heart consists of everything. For it is said in ParTri 21:

Śiva, who extends from the beginning of the universe to its infinite end, is considered the supreme triad of powers.

Within the body of the syllable *sa* belonging to Brahmā, there are the worlds beginning from the principle of Earth (*dharātattva*) up to the principle of Māyā, which belongs to Kālāgni. And it is said: "By means of the vowel 'sa'," and so forth.
Whatever exists within that, established on the path of purity,
that subtle and pure [soul] soon partakes in divine knowledge.

By the power of the Blessed One, it reaches the crown of the head in no time at all. How so?
Parātrīṃśikā 23:
That which impels it is to be known as Śiva, the omniscient Supreme Lord;
he is all-pervading, stainless, clear, satisfied, self-abiding, and pure.
