Śiva alone is the impeller of that.
And he is not merely unknowable, but is indeed to be known.
It extends its own objects and its own modes of consciousness;
all of this has indeed been determined in detail.
Having thus explained it in detail, he concludes with the essential meaning:
"Just as the great tree exists within the banyan seed in the form of a potentiality..."
In this way, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.
Thus, for one who knows this according to reality, initiation leading to nirvāṇa occurs without doubt, even if it is devoid of oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter.
It has been stated here that, for the time being, nothing exists;
yet the universe is the very self of the universe.
Consequently, just as within a banyan seed the sprout, the trunk, the leaves, the fruit, and so forth, exist in a form appropriate to them, so too does this entire universe reside within the heart.
Such thorough knowledge is itself the initiation into nirvāṇa free from doubt, as it has been said:
"This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva."
[Spandakārikā 2.7] Thus, although other forms of initiation might also bestow enjoyments,
this thorough knowledge alone is initiation in the true sense; therefore, it possesses the quality of being supreme among all here.
This is because it is superior even to the Kula scriptures.

For just as on the marks of a scale, even when the measurement increases higher and higher, there is an infinite difference in the magnitude of the rise and fall, so too, among the successive levels of reality (*tattva*), there is an infinite difference in space, time, experience, and consciousness; thus it becomes increasingly superior.
It may even exceed thirty-six [categories].

And since initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed consciousness itself, it has been stated: "A hero (*vīra*) or a yoginī who have entered into this very consciousness are favored by the form of the Reality (the *Tattva*) as determined to be the Lord Parabhairava—the Lord of the wheel of twelve deities consisting of the rays of the internal and external senses, which are of the nature of Māyā and perpetually arisen from one's own and other existences—and thus they are not [merely] those who have performed [ritual] initiation."
Thus,
it has been extensively determined through both detailed exposition and summary how the unsurpassed state (anuttarapada) exists precisely by way of not abandoning the form of the higher [stages].
Now, however, this must be stated:
It is said in the scriptures:
"Having assumed human bodies, those Supreme Lords remain concealed;
they worship the threefold object within the heart, even though it is devoid of power."
Thus [it is said]. How, then, is there meditation upon this?
Nevertheless, because it is unsurpassed, it must also be cultivated here due to its very nature of being unsurpassed.
Desiring to resolve the inquiry as to how that [cultivation] occurs, he introduces another text.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and likewise upon the body,
and having tied the topknot consecrated twenty-seven times with the mantra, [one should proceed].
One should perform the binding of each of the ten directions individually, having first struck three claps with sound for the pacification of obstacles. (ParTri 27)
Then, one should sprinkle with water consecrated by reciting the Śikhā-mantra the appropriate number of times;
subsequently, all the offerings, beginning with flowers, should be placed in order upon either the Liṅga or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The preparation of the seat is performed with a flower consecrated fourteen times;
there the hero should worship the emanation, and then once again the seat.
Having encapsulated the emanation, one should thereafter begin the worship, [visualizing the deity] fully complete with all principles and adorned with all ornaments. (ParTri 30)
One should worship the Goddess Maheśānī, consecrated with twenty-seven mantras;
thereafter, one should honor her with fragrant flowers according to one's ability. (ParTri 31)
One should worship with supreme devotion and offer oneself as well.
Thus is sacrifice declared; this same rule applies to the fire-ritual as well. (ParTri 32)
The crown of the head and the other [centers] externally appear in their appropriate forms;

yet in reality, they are nothing other than the manifestations of the expansion of consciousness— the essence of which consists of will, knowledge, and action— belonging to the lords (Īśāna and the rest) whose true nature is the fivefold reality beginning with space and ending with earth, as designated by the Supreme Brahman, according to the evidence of the Mantras.
Just as the mantras are: 1) for the head of Īśāna, 2) for the face of Tatpuruṣa, 3) ...
To the Aghora-heart, 4) to the Vāmadeva-secret, 5) to the Sadyojāta-form.
In this regard, there are two forms consisting of the non-differentiation of these five, namely the opening and the conclusion;
and in the middle, when the differentiation of the five shines forth, each one possesses a fivefold nature, resulting in twenty-five.
It is precisely here that the *mālinī* and other mantras enter.

The three goddesses, having each attained a ninefold nature through their union with the triad beginning with *icchā* (will), further assume a threefold state by virtue of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal; thus, they are remembered as twenty-seven. Through the heart-seed (*hṛdbīja*) [of the deity], there occurs a "binding"—that is, identity whose essence is the non-differentiation of all things—with that which is the sovereignty consisting in the mental construction of the entire range from the crest (*śikhā*) down to the foundation (*dharaṇi*), and which is figuratively designated by the forms of supreme consciousness, intellect, touch, breath, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the external world.
Even when taken individually, such as the head and so forth, all [parts] beginning with the face are mutual qualifiers;

and this has already been established by the determination that everything has everything as its self-nature (*sarvasarvātmakatva*). Those very things being pointed out, such as pots and the like, are the directions (*diś*); and they are exactly ten from their own perspective.
Even there, this very thing—consisting of the act of making [the object] one's own—is the bondage;
and this occurs through the three *tālas*.
*Tāla* means establishment and rest.
In that context, the heart-mantra begins with the letter *sa*;
and those [vowels] together with the sound *sa* end in the *madhyamā*.
For "sound" (*śabda*) is indeed the act of sounding (*śabdana*).
And it has been stated many times that this [Madhyamā] is indeed the middle state because it consists of the remainder of Vaikharī.

Furthermore, this is the peace— the identity with the ocean of Bhairava of non-duality— of the stains consisting of the waves of differentiation, whose essence is the contraction characterized by fragmentation, within the undivided Supreme Self which is the nature of non-differentiation.
As the venerable Śrī Somānanda said:
"May Śiva, who has entered into our very form, perform by means of his own power— the power that is *namaḥ*— the removal of the self from the self for the sake of the Transcendent Self."
Thus [Śivadṛṣṭi 1.1].
In this very manner, water consecrated twenty-seven times constitutes the ritual for the vessel of offering (*arghapātra*).
Here, "water" refers to everything that is essentially the liquid nature of the Heart.
Because it is unconfined and because it bestows non-constriction, the *puṣpa* has been explained. And as for the *liṅga*: it is that wherein the moving and the unmoving are dissolved (*līna*).
This too has already been determined:

in the act of sitting within the reality that is the self of the universe, the fact that both the locus— the seat— and the agent are conceived through their own sovereignty is expressed by the fourteenth vowel, *au*.

It has already been stated that this very [reality] has the form of a trident. Emission (*sṛṣṭi*) consists of the identity with everything from *A* to *KṢa*; it is the Heart, Power, and the Secret—this is its heroism (*vīratva*).
For this very reason, the entire seat (*āsana*) is also located right there.
Because the substratum and the thing contained therein are mutually of one and the same nature, as it has been said:
"The Self abiding in all beings...
[Bhagavadgītā 6.29a].
And so forth. "Enveloping" (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) refers to the creation [of the phonemes] from *a* to *kṣa*, both individually and in their entirety, by means of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdayabīja*).
Because there is manifestation within the Supreme Reality itself and because of reabsorption, there is no infinite regress; this has already been stated.
Furthermore, the enveloping of creation consists of the nature of bliss arising from the agitation of the union of both.
The utilization of the substances arising from that [state] is also [included].
Here, the suffix *ktvā* refers merely to the sequence of the cognition of the words.
"Fullness" (*pūrṇatvam*) means being thoroughly non-different from all principles (*sarvatattvaiḥ*), perfectly, and irreversibly.
And everywhere, even in a single atom, that which is the universal filling and the universal appropriation— namely,

the determination of the state of being a single-savoring whole (*ekarasa-avayavin*) by means of all the limited subjects (*pramātṛ*), such as pots, pleasure, animals, humans, Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Mantra, and Sadāśiva, each with their respective constituent measures— is indeed already established.
For this very reason, meditation on specific forms, weapons, and so forth, is not mentioned here.
Because it is something to be constructed;
if it is asked, "How can one who desires to ascend and who seeks these three goals actually ascend?", [the answer is: to whom does this state of being a seeker belong?
Let him then not ascend.

Let him instead rely upon the very procedures of the *Siddhātantra* and other such texts, wherein the meditations and other practices are delineated with their limitations precisely according to that [limited] intention;
for he is indeed not authorized in the uncontracted state of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
This indeed is the yoga that is eternally arisen.
Fragrance, flowers, and so forth have been determined.
The word "yathā" is used in the sense of "together with."
And the third [verse] is stated in that very same place:
"One should worship with the supreme [consort] herself, whose form is the heart.
How?
By means of devotion— characterized by the soul’s inclination toward entering into identity with Him—
and by means of devotion consisting of the self-constructed distinction between the worshiper and the worshipped;
for it is He Himself who is manifested as the object of worship.
The distinction here is that he is the ultimate reality of independent consciousness itself by virtue of the power of unsurpassed sovereignty, and is not insentient like a jar or similar object.
Thus it is said in the Śrī-Pratyabhijñā:

Q: By virtue of His sovereignty over the self that is liberated through sovereignty, and because He is non-dual in nature, the Lord creates [the world] through volitions such as those of Īśvara and causes it to function.
[Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.16] Thus, by means of devotion (*bhakti*) and figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*) is indicated through worship (*pūjana*).

In all ritual actions, there is the recognition of such a nature because it is the means (*upāya*), just as in the mastery of illusory phonemes there is the entry into the potency of those very phonemes, as in the case of written characters.
One should offer oneself,
because there is no other object to be offered;
and in this way, one should cause oneself alone to experience the unsurpassed state completely and without remainder.
In this context, the optative (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) according to the supreme reality (*anuttarasattā*),
for it has been stated that [the self] exists as being constantly of such a nature;
however, according to the perspective of devotional practice (*upāsā*), it is used even in the sense of injunction (*niyoga*) and so forth.
Thus, that which is everywhere and always known as "manifestation" (khyāti)—consisting of the unfolding of the ultimate, pure, and auspicious (śiva) nature—is itself the sacrifice (yajana).

This is because it consists of the worship of the deity of supreme Bhairava-consciousness, and because it effects a state of perfect identity with Her; and because it involves the renunciation (dāna), which is the cessation of the limited sense of ownership over one's own self in all things, and the bestowal of the supreme ownership of one's own nature, which consists of the full, dense mass of consciousness that is Śiva-Śakti.

This indeed is the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*): from the internal burning—that is, from the oblation—into the great splendor of Supreme Bhairava, which is perpetually kindled by the friction-sticks of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) agitated by the union with Śiva; a splendor that is intensely blazing due to its proficiency in devouring the fuel of all objective categories and the seeds of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and which possesses the abundant heat of the clarified butter consisting of great attachment to all things.
The intended meaning is that this very procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya) extends up to the initiation (dīkṣā), and there is no other separate one;
this mantra, which is the thorough knowledge of one's own true nature, is the ultimate reality.
This is initiation, this is sacrifice, and this is also the unsurpassed ritual action.

For this very reason, it was stated earlier that whereas in other systems the practice of mantra-worship and so forth is transcended by the subsequent section on knowledge (*jñāna*), it is not so here.

That which was stated in the aphorism, "The Unsurpassed is also beyond the Surpassed" (*uttarasyāpy anuttaram*), has been fully established by this concluding portion of the text, because the sacrifice and initiation rites are of the nature of the Heart itself, and that [Heart] is unsurpassed.

Furthermore, the venerable Somānanda-pāda has described all the rites, such as the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, with the intention of demonstrating their indivisibility through the principle of being the "all-enduring" (*sarvasaha*).

In such cases, even the division of limbs, the heart, and the various types of *dhūlis* (dust-particles) are consistent with that [system's] form; nothing here is contradictory, nor is it unestablished, nor does it exist [as something alien], nor is it dependent upon lower scriptures by virtue of being subsumed under them—this is essentially already determined. What, then, occurs through such worship? This is what follows.
ParTri 33ab:
One who has properly performed the ritual of worship attains success by remembering the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

Thus, even amidst worldly activities, by constantly remembering the seed-syllable, one has effectively performed the ritual of worship through that very remembrance alone—preeminently, that is, by surpassing other scriptures from the various *kula* traditions down to the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava systems.

Enveloped in the form of the Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka, one whose grand display of creative play (*bhāva-krīḍā-ḍambara*) is fashioned by the power of the wonder of the consciousness of oneself and others,

becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) according to the previously stated principle; thus, it is said that this is a matter of direct experience (*anubhava*) alone, revolving [within itself], and not anything else— this is what is meant by "recollection" (*smaraṇa*).
It is exactly thus in the Śrīmata scriptures:

even a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), though his heart has not yet entered the essence of the reality of vigor (*vīryasattāsāra*), attains the power of the mantras of reality known as "the Heart" (*hṛdaya*) by correctly recollecting the seed-syllable through the majesty of the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*);
he achieves perfection preeminently, solely through the majesty of the sequential worship.

Through the excellence of gradation, one either attains the potency of the mantra—which is of the nature of the Heart—either spontaneously or from the lotus-face of a gracious Guru-Bhaṭṭāraka, and thus becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
In this regard, the worship of the gatekeepers, the retinue, and the Guru neither adds a merit nor incurs a defect; for this very reason it was described by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda.
Here, however, the Kulaparvans and the Pavitraka constitute the perfection of the ritual procedure of worship.
That wherein everything shines within, and which shines everywhere—that alone is the throbbing reality; for that is the one supreme Heart, O wise ones. //1//
Like a female donkey or even a mare, she rejoices in her heart after having simultaneously expanded and then withdrawn the world, which is her own source of birth.
Likewise, one should worship within the heart of the *suṣumṇā*, which is the locus of both great joys, the throbbing heart characterized by emanation. // 3 //
Whether one is meditating, remembering, reflecting, or acting anywhere at all, that from which one attains rest and the heart exults is indeed that [reality]. (4)
That which is this supreme, conceptualizing knowledge is indeed one alone;
within it are the principles (tattvas), the expansion of the worlds, and the Mothers beginning with Śiva, who are the bound souls (paśus).
Making their own respective internal natures— which are indeed variegated— the ultimate reality,
they seek that supreme consciousness which is variegated.
Even regarding the knowledge of the ten substances, actions, and places, and so forth, his constant worship consists of proceeding with total confidence and without any doubt. (7)
In this Trika teaching, it is declared that perfect realization arises from worship here through the mere sequential worship along with the Kula festivals and the sacred threads (pavitraka). //8//
As it has been said:
"Just as the body is the seed of creation for fluids, so the Trika scripture is the seed of creation for all teachings; Bhairavī is the state of all liberations."
Q: Attainment through devotion, the heroic conduct of vows, and likewise, within the sacred festivals, the family festivals in the Teaching; Q: [these are the marks].
Q: For the completion of all sacrifices, there is the *pavitraka*.
Those who do not perform the *pavitraka* four, three, two, or even once [are at fault].
Q: "Those who do not know the *kulaparva* do not find their vigor flourishing.
Thus, the unsurpassed nature has been determined in detail.
Where there is no occasion for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth,
there is merely *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment), culminating in the firmness of realization characterized by a heart-pleasing, intense wonder; in such a case,
one places [the practice] upon the foremost stream of means among those seeking perfection (*siddhi*), though yoga must be explained [separately] for them.

Even when the accomplishments (*siddhis*) of the yoga of perception are brought about through one's own autonomy, although they follow the constraints of worldly convention, they do not transcend the constraint that consists of the Lord’s supreme arrangement;
as it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Nevertheless, for the sake of the work of painting, a means must be stated out of necessity."

Thus it is said. Even in that case, there is no fragmentation whatsoever of the unsurpassed nature, because even the desire for the attainment of what is seen, the effort, the practice, the acquisition thereof, the fruit, and the resting therein are essentially one with the Supreme.

However, from the perspective of one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), this [state] is called a "weak descent of power" (*manda-śaktipāta*) because it is characterized by a state of being largely incomplete.
The remainder of the treatise proceeds to define that path of yoga:
"The seed-syllable, devoid of beginning and end, blossoming and situated in the midst of the lunar days."
One should meditate upon that which resides within the heart-lotus and constantly practice the portion of the Moon.
This very seed of the heart is without beginning or end because it is devoid of the coming and going [of breath] due to the absence of a lamp [of thought], and because it is perpetually arisen.
That same [seed], expanding, has attained fullness;
it resides in the midst of the lunar days (tithis) because it is the heart.

One should meditate upon that very [reality] in the bulb (kanda) or the secret place, which has assumed the state of a lotus characterized by the qualities of contraction and expansion, just as in the heart. Furthermore, he describes its meditation:

one should cast or project the lunar portion consisting of sixteen digits in the form of filaments all around; and by means of the digit situated in the pericarp of the heart of this full moon, [one should project it] to its own respective end of the twelve.

Having received the touch of nectar brought from the source where the flowers and other [offerings] arise, he is sealed by the *kākacañcupuṭa-mudrā*, characterized by the kissing [of the breath] following the emerging *nāda*. Then, his moon—the body—filled by the drinking of the nectar churned from the *nāda* flowing forth from the heart, which has blossomed through tasting the cool essence of nectar approaching it, becomes composed of the rising digit of the sun, resting solely upon the vowel-less letter *sa*. His body is graced by horripilation, trembling, tears, shaking, and paralysis.
"One should practice thus," says Bhaṭṭadhaneśvaraśarman.

One should inwardly deposit into the heart the mere letter *Sa*, devoid of beginning and end, and free from the sixteen vowels starting with *Ā* and the lunar dates (*tithi*s), by means of the sequence of swallowing the *kalā*s (energetic digits), like the drawing up of water through a tube.
Simultaneously, one should [place it] within the moving, trembling, and vibrating Mūlādhāra, the triangle, the auspicious bulb (*kanda*), the heart, and the facial mudrās.

Thus, having rendered it devoid of beginning and end— by means of the swallowing of the network of lunar and solar digits (kalās) that has dissolved through the attainment of the streams of slow, medium, very fast, and even more intense [recitation]—

this seed-syllable is separated from its initial and final components, namely the vowel *au* and the consonant *sa*, with respect to the Mātṛkā; it is one whose power (*vīrya*) has been mastered through the application of the method of analytical separation.

One should meditate upon the sixteenfold nectar-portion of the moon within the heart-lotus— that which is the constant, emission-natured middle of the fifteen expanding lunar days (tithis), which is itself devoid of a lunar day, the seized time that is the sixteenth, and which proceeds even beyond that as what is called the "seventeenth digit. One should contemplate that sixteenfold immortal portion of the moon in the heart-lotus.
"One should practice that very [state] constantly," so say our teachers.

For the Lord Soma is so called because he exists through the agitation of the union consisting of the coalescence with the Blessed Lady Umā, which has the nature of churning the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Of him—the whole (*avayavin*) who comprises all states of existence and whose essence is the perfect "I-consciousness"—blue, pleasure, and so forth are parts (*aṃśa*).

Thus, one practices in this way: that which is contemplated as the truth is indeed this "heart-recitation" (hṛdayajapa) which is eternally arisen; it revolves again and again by means of the rosary of the axle of the wheel of the cycles of creation and withdrawal that turn toward one's own essential nature.
[The use of] the optative suffix (*liṅ*) here expresses possibility.

Others, however, [hold that] having caused [the breath] to shine forth in the form of the sun within that thirty-six-finger-length movement from the heart-center to the end of the twelve-fingers (dvādaśānta),...

Having rested for half a *tuṭi* externally, there occurs the rising of the lunar digit (*somakalā*) in the form of emission, which is imperishable and called "immortal" (*amṛta*). In each successive *tuṭi*, measuring two and a quarter finger-breadths, as each lunar digit is filled, it becomes full in the fifteenth *tuṭi*. At that point, it is full within the heart-lotus, and there too, one rests for half a *tuṭi*.

Thus, when the movement consists of sixteen *tuṭis* and measures thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*), one should practice the absorption of the digits (*kalāgrāsābhyāsa*). Having taught this and so forth, [the Master] explained that at this stage— one which is devoid of beginning and end because it does not set— one should meditate by means of repeated cultivation upon the seventeen-fold [reality], having dissolved within the center of the heart-lotus the lunar portion in the form of the *visarga*, which is inherent within the unfolding second [digit] and the others.
All of this should be considered entirely logical; and in this regard, an infinite exposition through repetition is indeed appropriate because it is a *sūtra*, as it has been said:
"A *sūtra* is so called because it threads together infinite meanings."
"The *Triṃśikā* is a supreme sūtra," so say the teachers. This applies likewise to the previous verse-sūtras as well. To the question, "What occurs when there is such practice? he says:
Whatever desires one may long for, those very desires one shall swiftly obtain;
from this, omniscience becomes manifest, without a doubt. (ParTri 34)

Thus, through such practice, whatever one desires, that very thing one attains without delay, by means of the force and exertion of a specific surge of will arising from the power of a heart that consists of all such things, and through the enthusiastic energy of repeatedly practicing the stabilization and ascension within that state.
What need is there for more?
Having stated everything—that omniscience, which is the nature of Supreme Bhairava, is attained by means of this very body—it is concluded.

For it has been stated repeatedly that Bhairava-hood consists in attaining the reality of Akula, which is the state of rest at the ultimate point of the expansion [of consciousness] during its withdrawal.
This is the concluding passage.
Thus, the attainment of the fruit of the mantra is this Rudrayāmala;
through the practice of this, perfection and omniscience are attained. (ParTri 35)
In this way, the fruit of the mantras belonging to other scriptures and of their phonemes is obtained, and not otherwise;
thus [ends the section] on the conclusion.

As for the *yāmala*—the union—of Rudra and Rudrā, it begins from the expansion of the self-reflection (*svarūpāmarśana*) consisting of questions and answers in an undifferentiated state, and extends as far as the manifestation of hundreds of external creations and dissolutions that are infinite and beyond counting.
This very [state] is indeed withdrawn into the Unmanifest (akula); this is the conclusion regarding discriminative discernment (prasaṃkhyāna).
"Omniscience arises from the practice of this"—this is the conclusion regarding the fruit of yoga.
For this is eternally manifest for all; may there be auspiciousness!

Thus, he whose lotus-feet are the beloved bees for the illustrious Maheśvara—who is intent on uplifting the people who have sought refuge—composed this commentary, which contains an investigation into the secret of the Trika, having received his birth from Cukhalaka of Kaśmīra. //1//
Who could forcibly weigh this glorious Śaiva doctrine, saying "it is only this much," when its words are unconfined?
Yet, that which has appeared to me shines within the Self of all; therefore, the wise should not turn their backs on it. // 2 //
This work brings about correct knowledge free from wavering for the ignorant or for those possessed of doubt and error;
and for those who have already attained firm conviction, it establishes a harmonious foundation within the heart.
One who has ascended to this synthesis of meaning and aesthetic essence, whose heart has reached a state of steady flow, should reflect even further than this. //3//
If it were superior, even that would not be tolerated; this is not the staircase for one desiring to ascend to that stainless state. //4//
In Kaśmīra, there was a preeminent minister of King Yaśaskara named the illustrious Vallabha, a twice-born man whose form was renowned for its excellence and who was of noble lineage.

His own son, Śrī Śauri, became a worthy recipient of the path of universal fame through his complete array of virtues; he was a singular ocean of jewels consisting of meditation upon the feet of the Child-Crowned Lord (Śiva). //5//
She is the abode of virtue, the source of another’s renown, the ground for the blossoming of humor, and the birthplace and dwelling of compassion for the entire world;
she is his illustrious companion named Vatsalikā, whose inner being overflows with devotion as her mind expands in the praise of Śaṅkara. //6//

His very self was one who had realized the creation and sustenance of the world; a twice-born man named Karṇa, whose sole delight was in the meditation, worship, and contemplation of Śaṅkara, who, having abandoned attachment to sense-objects even in childhood and youth, now resorts to this firm path of inquiry that uproots the cycle of existence. (7)
My own brother, whose mind is firmly established in the teaching of Śiva, named Manorathagupta, desires the Supreme Self;
he wishes to discern the entirety of the scriptures and tantras in order to attain the supreme state of Śiva for the sake of shattering worldly existence. (8)
Delighting solely in the Śiva scriptures and proficient in grammar, logic, and epistemology,
he was named Rāmadeva, his noble birth adorned with excellence.
May this exposition of the path, composed by me with a heart deeply rooted in performing what is dear and beneficial, lead to the attainment of auspiciousness for all. (10)
Having attained birth there within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), he of noble lineage entered [the land] known by the name Atrigupta—
the regions of glorious Kashmir whose borders had been purified by countless manifestations of the Moon-crested Lord.
Born from Varāhagupta, who was descended from that great lineage, [he entered the land].
He who was averse to the affairs of saṃsāra, whose mind was fixed solely on Śiva, was named Cukha. //12//

Therefore, having distinguished the entire collection of categories and having attained the state of the body purified by the Supreme Lord, Abhinavagupta—having obtained fearlessness—has caused this secret reality of Trika to enter [into the world]. 13.
As for those whose hearts are barren of solitude, a mere salutation is better for them; others may indeed seek solitude, yet they have not reached its further shore—fie on those dullards!

But as for that other person who stands firm in the conviction of the path whose essence is profound reflection—even if such a one is but a single individual among a hundred thousand, he alone may bring my effort to fruition. (14)
For those who even possess the indolence to distinguish their own selves [from the world], such prayers will yield no fruit from others; they are merely self-inflicted torment.
But for those of steady intellect who exert themselves to discern this entire universe, I have offered this respectful prostration with my head to entreat them. 15.

Wandering about themselves, those of dull intellect cause the circle of deluded living beings to wander as well; having made them their own, they bind them firmly with the fetters of abiding in the designations of the *guṇas*.
Seeing thus that these cattle follow after others who have set out for the task of bearing a heavy burden, I have fashioned this trident of knowledge to sever their bonds. (16)
Even by many who considered themselves teachers of reality, I alone have been led astray—those whose tongues did not even touch the two syllables "tat-tvam" (That-Thou). //17//
The glorious Lord Śambhu, the Supreme Sovereign, whose heart was moved by compassion to uplift those who have sought refuge, has appointed me to this reality. 18.

Having contemplated the doctrine of the venerable Somānanda, which has entered as if of its own accord into my heart that distinguishes the stainless state of ultimate reality, I have composed this work.

O Goddesses, who are filled with an overflowing abundance of bliss shining through your diligent movement within the wheel of the heart, and whose upward-pointing shafts of wisdom are skillful at severing the millions of bonds that bind us!

This [teaching], which removes the arising of fear regarding existence, has been perfectly woven into you through mind, speech, and body; therefore, go forth, for it shall forcibly bring about immediate clarity of faith in my heart. //20//

Having entered into the state of a teacher, I have been appointed by you to the sequence of duties such as exposition; therefore, O Goddesses, who are established in the skillful movement of that wheel, please forgive this fickleness of my speech and mind. (21)
This *Tattvavivaraṇa* on the *Paratriṃśikā* is completed.
This *Triṃśikā* has been analyzed in nineteen hundred [verses];
it shall shatter the knots in all the Trika scriptures.
The work of Abhinavagupta.
